#5833. Donated solar project powers community center in unincorporated New Mexico village  Solar Power World’s Projects of Impact

A building that started as a one-room schoolhouse has through the decades expanded to become a lifeline for a New Mexico community far from any city infrastructure, and a recent solar installation has brought new resilience to this place.

Children run outside of Ojo Sarco, New Mexico’s one-room schoolhouse in a photo from January 1943. The structure still stands today as the Ojo Sarco Community Center. Credit: John Collier, Jr./Library of Congress

The structure housing the Ojo Sarco Community Center (OSCC) was founded in the early 20th century. Ojo Sarco is an unincorporated community home to about 300 people that is located about 43 miles northeast from Santa Fe.

“We have no political voice, really,” said Carol Miller, a grant writer and board member for the Ojo Sarco Community Center. “We’re pretty neglected. We’ve lost resources in the past. We were the first wave of people to lose our post office many years ago. Everybody has to commute pretty much for everything.”

That commute is about 40 minutes round trip for basic amenities, she said.

The community center has tried to fill in those resource gaps with services like a twice-monthly food bank, summer meal programs for kids, safety classes and outings for its residents, such as a night at the opera. The OSCC also recently met all the qualifications to be a state library.

PPC Solar, also known as Paradise Power Company, from Taos, built a 7.5-kW solar project paired with 10.6-kWh of LFP energy storage at the OSCC. The contractor built the array at no-cost to the community center. Every year PPC donates a solar array to a regional nonprofit organization, and after three years of applying, the OSCC was awarded the project.

CEO Daniel Weinman’s father founded Paradise Power Company in the 1970s, and the company has installed solar in off-the-grid communities since the start. Its PV donation program is built out of that tradition.

“We’ve always wanted to find a way to give back to the community,” Weinman said. “The best thing that we found — and we’ve been doing it for over a decade now — is doing an annual nonprofit donation system … We’ve had farming organizations, land conservation organizations, and it goes on and on. Really, it’s about finding the right fit. We wanted to make a good impact for this community center, and we felt resiliency was the best way to do that.”

Solar Power World spoke to both PPC Solar and organizers with the OSCC about what effect this solar project has had in the village since it was built in fall 2025.

Larry Miller, project manager and OSCC board member: I think it’s a transformative project for our small community. We like to talk about the history of the community center, and now this is part of it. If someone doesn’t notice the solar panels on the roof, we point it out to them. It’s integrated into our lives here.

Carol Miller: It’s lowered our electric costs, which is really important for us, because we’re such a shoe-string operation. We’ve had some fun talks with the community because they all know we’ll have the charging capacity. We still have internet available, even with the power out. All the kids that come to our library programs, they’re solar oriented. The benefit of this company and its staff just has ripple effects throughout our greater community.

PPC Solar donated a solar plus storage project to the Ojo Sarco Community Center. This array will keep power running in this facility that has become a haven for Ojo Sarco residents. Credit: PPC Solar

Preston Bastardo, sales and design, PPC Solar: The building itself had some challenges with mounting the array on the roof, but that just took some exploration in the attic and making sure that we could land things where we needed to. The building has two large areas, and so fo installation of batteries had some restrictions, there was a good mechanical closet that we were able to use for batteries. Then as far as backup circuits, we did a partial facility backup where we had a critical loads panel next to their main panel. I think everything went pretty smoothly.

Weinman: Well, it really goes back to our roots. In 1972, there was no technology supporting solar at the time. My dad was a pioneer in the industry and he really developed his own controls and safety protections and found used panels and used batteries and was bringing power to places where there was no power. Our house, for example, we started with kerosene lanterns. We didn’t have electricity until we had a solar power system, and it was really life changing.

Being able to build on that legacy and look at our community in that light and be able to offer systems like this to communities that need it — I think that really adds to that legacy and really is profound in a lot of ways. It feels great to be able to do this and be in a position where we can help others realize and experience the benefits of solar power. We want to continue to participate in any way we can.

Carol Miller: We’re a very old community and proud of it. And having worked with local businesses and our electrical co-op, we know it’s really the exception and not the rule because we own our power. Any technology that is shared equally in a low-income community has ripple effects beyond what I think some of us imagined a number of years ago. It’s for everyone.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5832. Westward Ho! First Trip Cross Country with Our New 2026 Tesla Model Y & Full Self Driving V14

We were headed west again for the 6th time, driving the ~1500 miles from our lake house in Northern Wisconsin to our winter home near the grandchildren in Northern Utah. We had totaled our 2019 Tesla Model 3 in an accident in May; therefore, this was our first road trip in our new 2026 Model Y running Full Self Driving V14. As usual, we were carrying two big ebikes on the back. We plan to pause in Utah at our home for a few days and then on to Portland, Oregon, and the Pacific Ocean.

The experience was quite different this time because of the new car and the significant upgrade to Tesla’s driving automation: Full Self Driving Supervised V14.3.12.

As we approached our first Supercharger in Wausau, Wisconsin, it looked like the navigation was taking us the wrong way. However, once we got to our normal exit, it was closed. We had to drive a few miles beyond it, do a U-turn, and come back. It cost us roughly an extra 5 miles. I’m going to have to learn to trust the navigation. The Nav knows about road closures like this and even traffic jams. Unfortunately, it doesn’t explain ahead of time why it is suggesting an alternate route.

Our first stop was at the Wausau, Wisconsin Supercharger next to the Hilton Gardens Inn on highway NN. In 7 years, we’ve never seen more than a few cars charging there. For the first time, the charging station was full (see photo below). It was Sunday after a big fall-colors week in Northern Wisconsin and many tourists were headed home. On our screen, it gave a charger wait time of five minutes. As we drove the last 100 miles to Wausau, our computer screen alternated between showing an unspecified wait time and as many as two stalls open.

When we arrived, it listed two stalls as open, but, in fact, for nearly the first time across the last seven years that we’ve been Supercharging, all eight stalls were full. However, here’s the good part: within less than five minutes, one of the cars pulled out and we were able to back into the empty stall. Then, the bad part: it was the slowest charge we’ve ever experienced. It was an older V2 hardware Supercharger where you need to share charging with the adjacent car. That meant that we were charging at only a 50-kilowatt speed for the whole charge. The total charge took about 40 minutes. However, after the bathroom break and walking our small rescue dog, Zuni, we only needed to kill about 15 minutes before setting off again.

The next stop was Menomonee, Wisconsin, halfway to Minneapolis and the charger was showing three empty stalls. Since, as I mentioned, we were traveling on a Sunday, a beautiful day, with full fall colors in the Northwoods, we found another Supercharger that appeared to be full (see below), but there was one stall empty and we pulled in. When we came east in mid-May, there were seldom more than one or two cars in any of the 12 Superchargers en route.

The Menomonee Supercharger has a newer Hardware 4 charger, so we were charging faster, at almost 100 kW during our whole charge. As we pulled out, there were about three cars waiting, but the line moved quickly. No one had to wait more than a few minutes. Then we were on our way to Minneapolis.

About 20 miles east of Minneapolis, crossing the Saint Croix River on the border between Wisconsin and Minnesota, half the lanes of the bridge were shut down. The navigation took us on a town of Henderson detour going on highways U and UU, then back onto the I-90 route across the bridge. It probably saved time avoiding the worst of the traffic backup because of the closure on the bridge. Then we were on an east–west route right through the center of Saint Paul–Minneapolis. Full Self Driving V14 with Tesla navigation found its way through the big city freeways perfectly.

As we left the Minneapolis Supercharger, we couldn’t get Full Self Driving to work! It said “FSD Temporarily Unavailable.” However, temporarily lasted for a very long time. We went through a long troubleshooting process with Ara (the Grok bot) and with Tesla Customer Service on the phone. Not only did FSD fail to work, but it was reporting a speed limit of 15 mph when the actual speed limit was 65 mph. First, we stopped, put the car in park, and did the two-scroll button reboot. No luck. Then we were instructed to use the menu to reboot the car. No luck. Then we tried to recalibrate the cameras as suggested, but it was nighttime and the calibration wouldn’t finish. Not only was FSD not working, but smart cruise control also failed to operate. However, after partial re-calibration of the cameras, it did restore smart cruise control.

On day two of our cross-country trip, we left Worthington in the southwest corner of Minnesota on I-90, passing through a huge wind turbine field (see below) with hundreds of turbines on the north side of the road just as we got into South Dakota.

A short time later, we saw a wind turbine tower factory with hundreds of turbine tower sections laid down as you see in the photo.

As we began our drive through South Dakota we had smart cruise control, but no FSD.

The first Supercharger stop in South Dakota was at Murdo. I went into the pharmacy in the adjacent supermarket and bought some medical tape and taped over the back camera. I did this because we found that, with our older car, strangely, taping over the back camera was the only way to get full FSD to work with bikes on the back.

We restarted the camera celebration, which had failed the night before in the dark. This time we observed the little gray steering wheel icon in the upper-left-hand corner of the screen. A blue circle starts at the bottom around the icon, and it progresses all the way around to indicate that the calibration is in progress. However, when it was almost complete, it started over at the halfway point. It oscillated back and forth a few times for almost an hour before it finally completed the calibration and we got FSD back! We had lost FSD for the better part of two days of our 1500-mile trip. Since we pay $99/month for FSD, will Tesla give us a refund?????

Our stop in the middle of South Dakota was at the Supercharger in Wall, home of the famous Wall Drugstore. See my wife and our Tesla with the bikes at the Supercharger in the photo below.

We charged in Wall, South Dakota, and drove another 80 miles to the wildlife loop at Custer State Park. There, “we ran with the bulls” — I mean, we ran with the bison (buffalo). We were driving right in the middle of a big bison herd, as you see in the photos below.

My wife spotted hundreds of pronghorns on our trip west, and the visit to Custer State Park would not be complete without seeing one, as well as feeding and petting the donkeys.

We made it by 8:00 pm to the tiny town of Lusk, Wyoming, where a four-stall Supercharger is across the street from the Pioneer Best Western where we spent the night. The next morning, we were in eastern Wyoming, where we were following double railroad tracks used to ship coal from the huge, high-quality, low-sulfur coal deposits in northeast Wyoming to power plants farther east.

“Coal Area — The Powder River Basin spans over 1,000 square miles, making it one of the largest coal-producing regions in the US,” Google shares. “Depth of Coal Beds — Coal beds in the region can be as thick as 250 feet, with only 120 feet of soil overburden.”

The photos below show one of the unit coal trains bringing coal from the Powder River Basin as we passed. Clean power is on the rise, but coal is still an important part of electrical generation in the United States.

Powder Basin coal is also going to the Dave Johnson power plant in eastern Wyoming that we passed. It is an 817 MW plant that was scheduled to shut down next year (2027). However, the Trump administration has “rescued” it and it won’t shut down or be converted to gas for at least a couple more years.

On the third day of our trip, FSD was working and we stopped to charge at Evansville near Casper, Wyoming. Then we passed Devils Gap, Independence Rock, and the pioneer handcart company memorial on our way to Rawlins. At Rock Springs, I left my wife at the TJ Max while I charged at the Tesla Supercharger 100 yards away. The final charger was in Evanston, Wyoming, and then we crossed the Utah border and passed Park City, Heber, and drove down Provo Canyon to our winter home in Lindon just north of Provo (30 miles south of Salt Lake City). It took three 500-mile days to make the trip.

Summary: Our new 2026 Tesla Model Y seemed to charge a little slower than our old Tesla Model 3 Long Range. However, it appeared to have longer battery range. This meant that we could often travel as fast as 80 mph, whereas previously we never exceeded 75 mph and occasionally had to slow down as low as 60 mph to make the next charger — in our old Model 3 with the bikes on the back. FSD was a pleasure, keeping the car precisely in the middle of the lane, passing cars, and returning to the right-hand lane just as I would do myself … except when FSD failed to work for a big part of two days during the trip. I’m 86, and it was a strain keeping the car centered in the lane and keeping a foot on the accelerator when FSD wasn’t working.

#5831. The Senate permitting bill holds promise but needs amendments

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Targeted changes can minimize the most negative consequences of the permitting bill’s overreaching provisions, writes former FERC Chairman Mark Christie.

Mark Christie is a former chairman of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and former chairman of the Virginia State Corporation Commission, and is the director of the William & Mary Law School Center for Energy Law and Policy.

Every true compromise in a polarized legislature contains candy for each side, but also requires each side to swallow some hairballs. In the Senate permitting reform bill (SB 5653), the true permitting reforms hold a welcome potential to get needed infrastructure built faster. The transmission provisions, however — which are not permitting reforms at all — contain some provisions that are indigestible if you care about rising consumer costs and respect for historic state authority over utilities.

The bill’s best transmission provisions seek to ensure that large-load customers pay the full costs they impose on the grid. The worst transmission provisions, however, can be fixed with the amendments described below. Before considering these amendments, it is important to understand that the Federal Power Act for nearly a century has recognized a clear and logical division between state and federal authority over the power grid: The states have authority over the siting and permitting of all physical assets within their borders, including generation and transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has authority over the rates for interstate transmission services and wholesale power sales.

The current Senate bill blows up this century-old balance of authority by giving FERC the sweeping power to order a transmission line built in any state, without regard to the state’s own decision on the project or the opposition of the state’s residents who will be directly affected. Congress has enacted so-called “backstop siting authority” before, most recently in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act in 2021, but Congress strictly limited the geographic reach of FERC’s backstop authority to narrow geographic corridors established by the U.S. Department of Energy and only after DOE made a finding that the national interest required the establishment of each corridor.

The Senate bill contains no geographic limits on FERC’s permitting power. It expands FERC’s authority to override the states to every square inch of the country, a breathtaking expansion of federal power at the expense of a core state function: the permitting and construction of utility assets within their own borders, projects that could have huge impacts on the lives of their residents.

Fortunately, targeted amendments can minimize the most negative consequences of the bill’s overreaching provisions. Here are three recommended amendments:

The bill allows FERC to order the construction of transmission lines based on a nebulous “public interest” standard. Such a standard is a blank check for FERC to approve trillions of dollars’ worth of transmission lines for whatever reason a presidential administration finds is in the “public interest,” as long as FERC adds general findings of some reliability improvements or consumer benefits, which can be claimed for every transmission line ever proposed. In the short term, FERC could use the bill’s grant of new authority to order transmission lines built to serve hyperscale data center development, a Trump administration priority. A future FERC could find that the public interest requires trillions of dollars of new transmission to meet “Net Zero” climate goals.

So my first recommended amendment is to remove the “public interest” and other general criteria, and instead require that FERC must find that the proposed line is the optimal solution to meet a proven reliability need at just and reasonable rates, compared to alternative solutions.

My second amendment addresses the critical role of states in cost allocation. FERC Order 1920 guaranteed to states in a multi-state region the right to reach an agreement on cost allocation for regional transmission projects and have that agreement submitted to FERC. The Senate bill should add an explicit guarantee that for regional transmission projects the states in each region have the right to agree on cost allocation and FERC shall presume such state agreement is just and reasonable.

My third amendment concerns one of the most onerous and frankly insulting provisions in the Senate bill. When we at FERC implemented the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act’s backstop siting authority, we gave each affected state one full year to conduct its permitting proceeding before FERC would start its own backstop proceeding. That allowed the state to develop a factual record and issue a decision within a reasonable period of one year.

The Senate bill allows FERC to start its backstop proceeding simultaneously with the state proceeding. That effectively renders the state proceeding meaningless, and states will perceive it exactly that way. Why should a state spend its time and limited resources on its proceeding when FERC is already doing its own? Any evidentiary record developed in the state proceeding may not even be available to FERC before it overrides the state. This provision in the Senate bill is nakedly punitive and overreaching and should be amended to give the states one full year to act before FERC can begin its own backstop proceeding.

Even if you don’t care about respecting state authority, you should care about the bill’s impact on consumers already struggling to pay their power bills. Over the past decade, transmission has been one of the fastest-growing drivers of power bill increases. The Senate bill as drafted could result in literally trillions of dollars of new transmission being ordered by FERC to serve whatever policy goals a president wants. These costs will flow right into consumers’ monthly bills.

Every compromise offers candy and hairballs. With these amendments, the bill can be made a lot sweeter.

#5829. “Everything Trump Touches Dies” — A Warning For America

In August 2018, Rick Wilson, a long-time GOP media consultant, published a book entitled Everything Trump Touches Dies. In it, he argued that MAGA and Trump will ruin the reputations, careers, and stability of the people and institutions that choose to align with him. Recently, Paul Krugman and Heather Cox Richardson published separate posts on Substack that bring Wilson’s warning forward to the present.

Krugman based his article on the writings of Robert Pape, author of the Substack Escalation Trap, who argues that, as the loss of control of the House and possibly the Senate becomes more likely, it is making Trump more dangerous than ever. Krugman wrote:

“It’s a well-understood proposition that the owners of businesses that are on the verge of going bust often engage in destructive behavior. And Trump is about to go bankrupt — not financially but politically. So he, like a failing businessman, has strong incentives to wreak havoc.

“Pape’s argument is basically a version of the phenomenon often called ‘gambling for resurrection.’ When a company is on the edge of failure, it makes sense for the owner to make highly speculative, even crazy investments that are highly likely to fail but might, just might, make enough money to pull the company back from the brink. After all, for the owner it’s heads he wins, tails his creditors lose.

“In Trump’s case, all indications are that his party is heading for defeat in the midterms. And while a normal president might be able to live with a Congress controlled by the opposing party, there has been so much corruption and malfeasance over the past two years that Democratic control of Congress, and the subpoena and investigative power that will bring, will have catastrophic consequences for Trump and everyone around him.

“So Trump has an incentive to do something — anything — that might shake up this election. Attacking Iran would probably lead to an even bigger Republican defeat, but it might, just might, rally Trump’s base enough to change the outcome. True, a president who cared at all about what is good for America wouldn’t pursue disastrous policies for the slim chance of saving his own political skin. But this is, after all, Trump we’re talking about.”

According to Richardson, the Wall Street Journal has reported that Vladimir Putin has proposed a meeting next month with Trump and China President Xi Jinping to decide the fate of Ukraine.

The report explained that “a three-way summit with China and the U.S. would cement Russia’s status as one of the world’s three great powers, a status Putin has sought since 2000 when he entered the Kremlin. Such a summit would formally acknowledge that the U.S. had broken from Europe and allied with Russia, a goal for Putin as he tries to take control of Ukraine.”

Richardson wrote, “After ten years of Trump insisting that reports of his cooperation with Russia were a hoax, here we are, watching one profoundly unpopular man tear apart the global system under which we have lived for eighty years in order to climb into bed with Vladimir Putin.”

Writing in The Atlantic, national security scholar Tom Nichols said, “The American commander in chief has abandoned the Western order, the most successful — and powerful — security arrangement in human history.” Richardson observed:

“This decision appears to have had nothing to do with the national interest of the United States…. Instead, Trump appears to have thrown out the world order because of his own personal interests, his admiration for Putin, his resentment of Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky, and quite possibly other factors that so far have remained obscured from the American public.

“Outrage over Trump’s actions has come from across the political spectrum,” she wrote. “Nichols notes that former federal prosecutor turned conservative commenter Andrew McCarthy wrote that Trump is giving Putin ‘aid and comfort.’ Those words echo Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, which defines treason against the United States, as ‘levying War against them, or in adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort.’

“McCarthy’s blistering article in the National Review on Saturday reminds readers that Putin is a murderous dictator who is actively supporting Iran’s military operations against the United States with both intelligence and drones and provoking U.S. allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. And yet Trump is siding with him against Ukraine, a U.S. ally. McCarthy demanded Congress hold ‘immediate hearings about this week’s shocking escalation of the Trump-Putin alliance.’”

Krugman warned that a cornered Trump may resort to what he calls “policy looting” by “using his remaining power to take actions that are both deeply unpatriotic and deeply unpopular, but fit his own preferences and prejudices. With nothing left to lose, he will be free to be his worst self — a malignant narcissist who instinctively supports authoritarians and is preoccupied with revenge against anything and anyone that threatens his fragile grandiosity.” In other words, a raging lunatic with access to the nuclear codes.

“Anyone who believes Trump will become more cautious, more moderate in the aftermath of midterm defeat just doesn’t understand the new political reality. The truth is that political bankruptcy will free Trump to pursue his true desires. And those desires are horrifying,” he wrote.

Left to his own devices, Trump is an existential threat to the United States that came into being in 1776. Don’t overlook the fact that the US Supreme Court has enabled and emboldened him, based on a legal theory known as “the unitary executive,” a creation of conservative groups like the Federalist Society that has no basis in the Constitution.

Richardson concludes her essay with this observation:

“The Framers of the Constitution thought they had designed a system that would prevent the rise of a tyrant. They believed U.S. representatives would be so fearful of a leader’s abuse of power that they would impeach any president who overstepped his authority, and that U.S. senators would be so jealous of their own power they would convict, and tyranny would not be able to take root.

“The Framers especially did not anticipate that senators, to whom they deliberately gave longer terms than they gave the president, would put party over country and stand aside as a president and his appointees captured the prerogatives of the Senate.

“But even given the evidence of the past ten years, it is truly astonishing to see Republicans, who for more than forty years have championed President Ronald Reagan for his stance against the Soviet Union, stand aside as Trump trashes the post–World War II system of global security in order to ally the United States with a Russian dictator.”

In the end, the people who fashioned the Constitution simply failed to anticipate the overwhelmingly corrosive influence of power, nor did they provide a way to rein in a madman. RIP, America. The world may never see the likes of you again.

#5828. Here's How Many Patients Fudge the Facts to Get Antibiotic Scripts

— Caregivers also reported misrepresenting kids' symptoms for antibiotics

More than one in four adults said they misrepresented symptoms to try to get antibiotics for themselves or their children, survey results showed.

Among 959 adults, 27.9% said they had misrepresented symptoms to their clinicians to get antibiotics for themselves, with 26% reporting that they had exaggerated their existing symptoms and 16.7% reporting that they had made up symptoms that didn't exist.

Notably, 76.9% of those who misrepresented symptoms at least once said they succeeded in getting antibiotics, noted Alistair Thorpe, PhD, of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, and colleagues in JAMA Network Open.

Among 236 caregiver respondents, 26.7% reported that they had misrepresented a child's symptoms to get clinicians to give them an antibiotic: 24.2% said they had exaggerated a child's symptoms, 23.6% said they had fabricated symptoms, and 19.1% reported doing both. Of note, 87.3% said they'd successfully received antibiotics, reported Thorpe and colleagues in a separate research letter in JAMA Network Open.

"Together, these findings suggest concerning patient-clinician dynamics characterized by patients not feeling taken seriously, unclear and inconsistent messaging about antibiotics and antimicrobial resistance, conspiracy-like beliefs about antimicrobial resistance, and symptom misrepresentation to obtain antibiotics," Thorpe and team wrote.

These results "signal a significant issue for health professionals making antibiotic prescribing decisions and for the fields of antimicrobial stewardship and public health," they concluded.

Blame for unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions extends beyond dishonest patients, cautioned Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in an accompanying commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness," Linder wrote.

For diagnoses for which antibiotics aren't appropriate, "prescribing antibiotics is medically incorrect and could itself be considered a form of dishonesty or lying mainly to assuage the patient," he noted. Beyond the potential danger to patients and the rise of antimicrobial resistance, "the more concerning negative externality of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing is, like lying, an erosion of trust."

Prescribing antibiotics that clinicians know "are more likely to hurt than help ... is an affront to clinicians' professional responsibility to our patients," Linder concluded. "Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest, even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

Conducted in early 2026, the online survey asked U.S. adults if they had ever exaggerated or fabricated symptoms to obtain antibiotics. Respondents were also surveyed about their reasons for their decisions.

Among adults who misrepresented symptoms for themselves, cold-like symptoms were most often exaggerated or faked (65.7% of respondents), followed by stomach symptoms (49.3%), joint or muscle pain (46.3%), and nothing specific (36.9%). Of the eight symptom categories, only one -- urinary symptoms -- "clearly justified antibiotic prescribing," Linder noted.

Among adults, reasons for misrepresenting their own symptoms included:

Factors associated with higher odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation to obtain antibiotics included often feeling that clinicians do not take their symptoms seriously (OR 2.19, 95% CI 1.49-3.22), believing that antibiotic resistance is a hoax (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.34-2.93), reporting more comorbidities (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.05-1.28), having higher lying acceptability scores (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.23-1.80), and needing help reading health materials (OR 2.40, 95% CI 1.62-3.54). In contrast, dislike of taking antibiotics (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81-0.99) and higher antibiotic knowledge (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.58-0.91) were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation.

Few patients had regrets about bending the truth to get antibiotics. Among adults, fewer than 30% said they regretted their action, and those who did were more likely to do so because of adverse effects or ineffectiveness than concerns about dishonesty.

Among caregivers who misrepresented a child's symptoms, 63.5% who reported that they lied about symptoms said they did so because they felt clinicians didn't take their child's symptoms seriously. That group was significantly more likely to misrepresent symptoms (adjusted OR 3.34, 95% CI 1.44-7.99), as were caregivers whose child had comorbidities (aOR 1.24, 95% CI 1.02-1.54), those with higher lying acceptability scores (aOR 2.06, 95% CI 1.33-3.31), and those with lower health literacy (aOR 2.50, 95% CI 1.06-6.05).

Caregivers with higher antibiotic knowledge scores had lower odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation (aOR 0.55, 95% CI 0.31-0.93).

Study limitations included the small number of survey respondents, who may not represent the U.S. population. Inaccurate reporting also may have led to underreporting.

#5827. Batteries Beat Norway’s Hydrogen Bulk Carriers on Cost in Two Modeled Routes

Norwegian shipping company GMI Group is moving ahead with four hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for coastal freight. In October 2026, PowerCell confirmed a follow-up order that brings the program to 24 marine fuel-cell units with 5.4 MW of combined installed capacity. The first two ships, rated at 4,000 deadweight tonnes, are planned for 2027, while two additional 3,000-tonne vessels are expected in 2029.

The project has real shipbuilding commitments and substantial public support. The question is whether hydrogen makes economic sense for the freight services these vessels will provide.

GMI says its design can deliver lifetime costs 9–10% below conventional ships. Its argument combines fuel cells, batteries, an efficient hull and wind assistance. Those are useful engineering features, but most are not exclusive to hydrogen propulsion. A diesel or battery-electric ship can have a similarly efficient hull and sails. The fuel and energy systems still need to be compared on equivalent terms.

I modeled two hypothetical 3,000-tonne coastal bulk services, covering 80 and 55 nautical miles, using comparable hull performance and operating requirements. Over fifteen years, hydrogen propulsion came out 50–58% more expensive than conventional diesel, even after assuming approximately €13.1 million in public vessel support was received upfront. Battery-electric alternatives were €11.64–14.13 million cheaper than the subsidized hydrogen vessels. These are scenario results, not estimates of GMI’s actual operating contracts.

The company has not published the route and commercial data needed for a direct assessment, and the model’s vessel acquisition prices remain important uncertainties. The battery alternatives were not the cheapest option under every assumption. In the central cases they cost somewhat more than diesel over fifteen years. Their advantage was the much smaller gap to conventional operation compared with hydrogen. Battery-electric propulsion also requires adequate grid connections, charging equipment and berth time, which cannot be assumed available at every Norwegian port.

Hydrogen has a different set of requirements. Renewable electricity must be converted into hydrogen, compressed, stored, delivered to the vessel and converted back to electricity in fuel cells. Those additional processes introduce energy losses and capital costs that efficient hulls and sails cannot erase. They matter particularly for short coastal voyages where a practical charging arrangement may be possible.

Norway is using substantial public funding to support the hydrogen ships. Norsk Hydrogenforum reports Enova awards totaling roughly €42.9 million for the four vessels. Additional public support has been awarded to GreenH hydrogen production projects. Announced grants are not necessarily fully paid, and a subsidy changes the allocation of costs rather than eliminating the equipment and energy required.

There may be coastal services where voyage length, available berth time or grid limitations favour hydrogen over batteries. That needs to be established through engineering and commercial comparisons, rather than inferred from the existence of a funded shipbuilding program.

Before further public commitments to compressed-hydrogen coastal freight, Norway should require credible battery-electric bids using vessel, charging and energy prices appropriate to the expected entry-into-service dates.

#5826. The industry races into Las Vegas for RE+

The largest tradeshow focused on the U.S. solar, storage and clean energy markets is back in Las Vegas for 2026. RE+ was the 24th largest tradeshow in the United States in 2025 by attendance, and this year’s showing (Nov. 16-19) is expected to be just as large.

The Formula 1 series will race the Las Vegas Grand Prix the weekend after RE+ concludes. Photos courtesy: F1 and the Las Vegas Grand Prix

The U.S. solar and storage industries have gotten so big that it appears only the Las Vegas Convention Center can accommodate a tradeshow bringing together nearly 40,000 clean energy professionals in one place. RE+ will be held at the Las Vegas Convention Center each November for the foreseeable future.

The convention center is tucked away from the main strip of casinos, but there is still plenty in the area to see and do. The site is also easily accessible, with a stop on the Las Vegas Monorail.

Conference education programming begins on Monday and sessions continue throughout the show at various stages on the exhibit hall floor. The exhibition opens on Tuesday.

Exhibitors will be spread across three halls in the convention center — the main entrance is at West Hall which extends via an over-street walkway to North Hall, and then Central Hall is accessed beyond a lobby area. #5825. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. #5824. A Referendum On Elon Musk And Transgender Rights — Who’d A Thunk It?

US voters rarely, if ever, get a chance to vote on someone whose name is not on the ballot, but this year is an exceptional one with Tesla CEO Elon Musk throwing millions at key races. In years past, Musk’s seal of approval would be a planet-saving badge of climate action honor for candidates seeking office. Now he’s just another highly privileged crank exercising his outsized financial power against transgender rights. Who’d a thunk it?

Coincidentally or not, Elon Musk’s highly personal vendetta against transgender rights has materialized against the backdrop of a corresponding focus in Republican Party campaign strategy, with one early hint being his “pronouns suck” message on Twitter in July of 2020.

Musk went on to buy Twitter and rename it “X” in 2022, and the rest is transphobic history.

Also coincidentally or not, the Republican Party has been hammering against human and civil rights for generations, but the razor-sharp focus on transgender persons did not bloom into full flower until 2021, after US President Donald Trump lost his first bid for re-election.

In the aftermath of Trump’s failed insurrection of January 6, the Party alighted upon transgender rights as a powerful tool in a coordinated campaign strategy aimed at ginning up the fevered emotions of voters already besotted with US President Trump’s “MAGA” propaganda during his first term in office.

In addition to working the conservative aisle of the US Supreme Court, the anti-transgender movement has focused on legislation introduced by state lawmakers (looking at you, Florida). Among the LGBTQ+ organizations tracking the bills is the organization is the Human Rights Campaign, which has identified a distinct shift in anti-transgender strategy during the 2020 campaign cycle.

All else being equal, transgender persons are an unlikely target for a national political campaign. According to one study, self-identified transgender persons over the age of 13 make up just 1% of the US population, with much of the self-reporting cohort under age 35. As for the much-ballyhooed danger of transgender-related surgery on minors, that is vanishingly rare to the point of not occurring at all according to a 2024 Harvard study. Somewhat ironically, the same study found a “substantially higher” rate of sex-affirming surgery among non-transgender minors and adults.

For that matter, Elon Musk is known to have availed himself of body-affirming treatments as an adult, but that’s a whole ‘nother can of worms.

Regardless of the numbers, the political payoff for anti-transgender activism is substantial. Prior to 2020, Republicans did not focus narrowly on transgender rights. Their attacks were a broad barrage against marriage equality for LGBTQ+ couples, as part of a relgion-centric campaign to eliminate legal and constitutional protections. Although this type of legislation continues to appear in statehouses, HRC identified a sharp rise in the number of bills specifically attacking transgender rights during the 2020 campaign cycle. The organization summarized its findings in a report last year, stating that “opponents of LGBTQ+ equality explicitly – and admittedly – began attacking transgender youth” (emphasis added).

In the report, HRC takes note of ADF (formerly Alliance Defending Freedom) and other anti-LGBTQ+ organizations serving as “bill mills,” that funnel pre-written legislation to state lawmakers in a coordinated campaign. So, if you’re wondering why gender-related health care for minors became such a hot button issue during the 2024 election cycle, alongside transgender participation in youth sports, there’s your answer.

Although some Democrats also contributed a share to the hate fest, the bulk of the coordinated anti-transgender campaign that poured out of state legislatures in 2021, and the following years, is credited to Republican lawmakers.

The anti-transgender strategy exceeded expectations in the 2024 election cycle, aided by a late-stage change in the Democratic ticket. Podcaster Joe Rogan, among other Trump-endorsing influencers, is also credited with swinging the Gen Z (ages 18-29) vote to the Republican Party, with spectacular results.

The public mood has soured since then, to say the least. Most people may or may not ever encounter a transgender person in their whole life, but they encounter Trump every time they go to fill up their car with gas.

Still, with the well known anti-transgender activist Elon Musk contributing almost half a billion dollars (and counting) to support Republican candidates in key races around the country, transgender rights are still on the ballot — and now the whole strategy is backfiring.

CleanTechnica’s Carolyn Fortuna took note of the Great Backfiring over the weekend, observing that “Musk’s blatant attempts to influence election results are getting a lot of recent analysis and condemnation.”

“US Federal Election Commission data revealed this week that Elon Musk has donated at least $445 million into Republican-aligned political action committees and groups since last year. Interestingly, it seems that Musk’s deep influence isn’t enough, and he is worried,” Fortuna explained.

“If Democrats win big on Tuesday in midterm elections, Musk insists US democracy will come to an ‘end,” she continued, citing this message on X last Friday, October 30, from Elon Musk:

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029.”

Despite Musk’s millions, the effort is having little effect in the run-up to Election Day. Take Texas, for example, where Musk has devoted his millions, and his amplified voice, working the anti-transgender message to support Ken Paxton for US Senate against the Democratic candidate James Talerico.

Don’t just take my word for it. The well known independent journalist Judd Legum is among those taking notice. “Musk is blanketing the internet with digital ads falsely accusing Democratic Senate candidates of supporting ‘taxpayer-funded sex changes for kids,’” Legum reported on September 23.

In Texas, the attack ads are just one prong of a transgender-centric attack strategy that includes raising “questions” about Talerico’s sexual identity. The Talerico campaign, for one, is having none of it. They are turning the anti-transgender strategy back on Musk. Nothing will be certain until the dust settles after election day, but so far Musk’s millions have failed to move the needle for Paxton in Texas, where according to late breaking polls Talerico leads by a slim margin.

As reported by Houston Public Media, Talerico has been regularly blasting Musk’s influence in the Texas midterms in campaign speeches, tying the world’s richest man to a Republican candidate who drags a considerable amount of scandal and corruption baggage.

As for Musk’s interest in Tesla, not to worry. Despite Elon Musk’s personal and political baggage, the iconic automotive startup continues to hold the #1 position in EV sales in the US by a wide margin. On the other hand, General Motors and Ford are rebooting their EV efforts in anticipation of a friendlier political environment next year and beyond. Other legacy automakers, including Toyota and Subaru, have also introduced new EV models to the US market this year. In addition, Rivian and other pure play EV startups are contributing to the rising competition against Tesla for EV sales in the US. Hold on to your hats…

#5823. AI, Digital Pathology in Early Breast Cancer Among Highlights at SABCS

— Virginia Kaklamani also previews studies on antibody-drug conjugates, endocrine therapy, and more

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital pathology in early breast cancer will be a major theme at the upcoming San Antonio Breast Cancer Symposium (SABCS), with new research exploring whether image-based tools can help determine which patients need chemotherapy or extended endocrine therapy.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Virginia Kaklamani, MD, DSc, of the University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center, who is co-director of SABCS, previews some of the early breast cancer research to watch at this year's meeting, including studies on novel antibody-drug conjugates and endocrine therapy, genomic studies, and a debate on the use of trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd; Enhertu) in the neoadjuvant versus adjuvant setting for HER2-positive disease.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

Hello, my name is Virginia Kaklamani from UT Health San Antonio, and I'm one of the co-directors of the San Antonio Breast Cancer Symposium.

So for this year's symposium, our 49th year, we're going to have a lot of really interesting abstracts, especially in the early-stage setting, looking at AI. So looking at digital pathology and how this digital pathology can actually help us determine who needs chemotherapy and who doesn't need chemotherapy, who needs extended endocrine therapy, and so forth. This is really a new era where we have a lot of tools available so that instead of taking a specimen, sending it to a laboratory thousands of miles away, and analyzing it, now with digital pathology, all we need to do is just take a picture and send that picture over and then that picture gets analyzed, and really the information that we get may actually be as good, if not better, than the information we get from doing genomic assays on specific tumor specimens.

So this is going to help, I think, in the future because it'll allow us to do these tests quicker and also cheaper. And we can do them from anywhere in the world, whereas right now these laboratories sometimes in certain countries have specific regulations.

So I think this is kind of the biggest news out of SABCS this year, but there's so many other things. We have new novel antibody-drug conjugates. We're going to be looking at endocrine therapy in the early-stage setting and so forth, and a lot of other genomic presentations that'll really help us treat our patients better.

This year we expect more than 11,000 people to come to San Antonio. We always have many medical oncologists, surgical oncologists, radiation oncologists, advocates. I think the strength of SABCS is the presence of our patient advocates and the inclusion of our patient advocates through the program and the different sessions that we have.

We have several special sessions that are looking at lobular carcinoma, looking at obesity and breast cancer, GLP-1 agonists, really the talk of the past -- what, 5, 10 years -- and how GLP-1s can help improve health in our patients with breast cancer, potentially also improve outcomes in our breast cancer patients.

So a lot of things happening in the symposium, from educational sessions, state-of-the-art sessions, debate. The big debate this year is going to be whether to give T-DXd in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting in patients with early-stage HER2-positive disease. So the 5 days that the meeting is going on is really going to be crazy, but it's going to be a lot of fun data to discuss.

#5822. Jackery Launches Explorer 100D Portable Power Station. Maximum Capability For Carryon Compatibility

Jackery just launched the Explorer 100D portable power station. This is Jackery’s smallest battery, giving a new level of versatility to power many of the devices people rely on most. Meanwhile, it integrates  the durability and safety people expect from Jackery’s larger models into a compact case.

The Explorer 100D has a capacity of 96 Wh (30,000mAh) which puts it just below the carryon limit for domestic and international flights. Meanwhile, up to 158 W of output is more than enough to charge a laptop. The 100D is compatible with advanced protocols including AVS, PD 3.1 and PPS, providing precise charging, particularly for Apple products.

The Explorer 100D measures 4.6” X 3.4” X 3.4”(11.6 X  8.3 cm X  8.5 cm), or about the size of a softball. It weighs 1.87 lbs. (850 g). This is a bit larger than the typical power bank, but much smaller than the typical solar generator. It is also smaller and lighter than the Explorer 100 Plus that it replaces, while also increasing in power output.

On the test sample model, I found the form factor very convenient. It is not small enough to fit in your pants pocket, but the rectangular case with rounded corners was easy to fit in a backpack or carryon bag. A cloth handle makes it easy to hold, and a shoulder strap is available. I had a credentials lanyard from a previous media event on hand, and it worked fine as a strap for the lightweight battery.

On the front of the battery are two 140 W USB-C ports and an 18 W USB-A port. The left USB-C port can both charge the battery and discharge to another device. The battery can also be discharged through the other two ports while it charges. The battery does not come with a charger, although a USB-C cable is provided. I was able to charge the Explorer 100D on a wide range of chargers, although lower powered chargers take a while to charge the large capacity battery.

The front display default shows battery charge percentage as well as input and output power. However, you can switch the display to also show power output to each port or battery health, cycles and temperature.

Unlike some of Jackery’s larger batteries, the 100D does not have cooling fans or vents in the case. The LFP battery is rated for 3000 full charge cycles, good for 8 years of daily use. This is far more durable than many Li-ion power banks, which commonly only offer a few hundred charge cycles. It is also a 50% improvement over the previous Explorer 100 Plus model that it replaces. Of note, while this model does comply with China’s strict CCC (China Compulsory Certification), the logo was not printed on the test model I received, although that may change in the future. Without the logo present, it could be taken away if travelling in China. However, the battery did have FCC and SGS certification printed on it, which are more relevant to most US customers.

The portable battery can function as a solar generator by accepting direct solar input up to 100 W. This makes it a bit different than many power banks. Solar panels connect through the USB-C charge port. which may require the purchase of an adaptor, depending on the panel used. Jackery’s lightweight, folding SolarSaga 100 Air could charge the battery in less than two hours. The battery can also take 12 V or 24V input from a car, boat or RV. Using a traditional USB-C charger, the Explorer 100D can accept up to 140 W of input power.

The Explorer 100D  test model came with 30% charge and reached a full charge in about an hour. While the battery was charging, I was able to charge my phone and another power bank off the output ports while the battery was charging. I initially charged the battery off the HomePower 1000 Plus V2, which has a 140 W USB-C output. With similar styling, it looked like a baby of the larger battery when placed on top. Of course, the battery would take longer to charge on lower power. However, it could be used to accumulate charge over time and discharge more quickly for a device like a laptop that needs more power than what may be available from a charge jack at a hotel room or airport.

While the battery will often be used to charge phones, the Explorer 100D ran my T-Mobile Wi-Fi router all day, with capacity left to charge my phone and tablet. When used with a laptop with a USB-C charge port, the small battery could power a remote office.

I was also able to run a small personal fan off of the Explorer 100D. With peak power draw at 5 watts, it didn’t pose much of a challenge for the battery. This would come in handy at an outdoor event or while fishing on a hot day.

On Halloween, I used the battery to power an old Bluetooth speaker for hours of handing out treats, while keeping our phones charged. The black and orange design fits well with the holiday decorations. By the end of the night, the battery still had over 90% capacity.

I also used the battery on a trip to an apple harvest festival. While charging ports were in short supply in the car, the Explorer 100D kept phone and camera batteries topped up. The rubber feet kept the battery from shifting around when placed on the center console.

The Jackery Explorer 100D launches as a two-unit bundle for $179.99 at select Costco warehouse locations from the start of November 2026. Individual units will then become available at Walmart for $99 on November 15th, just in time for holiday travel.

Frost & Sullivan recently named Jackery the World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand. Jackery leads in solar generator sales volume globally and has pioneered multiple innovations in portable power. The Explorer 100D is the latest example. The company has a focus on providing solutions for customer needs with durable products that have exceeded my expectations in testing. After trying the Explorer 100D, I also find it to be more useful than I originally expected, using it in a wide range of applications. While the Explorer 100D clearly is not going to solve all of the world’s energy problems, it provides another power option that meets the needs of many customers while integrating well with Jackery’s expanding range of solar and energy storage products. As Steven Wang, CEO of Jackery Americas puts it:

Power support is often most effective when it’s highly portable and backed by comprehensive compatibility and a long lifespan. Developed for peak productivity, the Explorer 100D represents years of honed design and feature implementation, while maintaining focus on the top-quality engineering and unmatched consistency that make Jackery portable power stations must-haves for work and travel. Thanks to that collection of refined expertise, it’s among the longest-lasting ultra-portable batteries ever.

I look forward to putting the Explorer 100D to the test during some upcoming travel over the next few months. I also look forward to seeing what Jackery comes up with next in versatile, portable power.

#5821. Another Surgical Treatment for Back Pain Fails in Rigorous Analysis

— Norwegian registry data show no benefit from spine fusion as part of decompression surgery

Spinal fusion added to decompression surgery in patients with spinal stenosis did not provide any added benefit versus decompression alone, Norwegian national registry data indicated.

With outcomes compared for 1,446 patients undergoing decompression alone and 806 having spinal fusion as well, no significant difference in Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores was seen a year later, according to James H. McAuley, PhD, of Neuroscience Research Australia in Randwick, and colleagues.

This is not the first study to question the utility of spinal fusion for patients with degenerative stenosis, the group noted in their report appearing in Annals of Internal Medicine. Earlier, prospective trials in Sweden and Norway found no improvement in disability when compared with decompression surgery alone, as did a smaller U.S.-based study (although the latter did show better quality of life with fusion). Moreover, these trials all showed a higher burden of complications such as bleeding with spinal fusion, along with prolonged operative time and increased costs.

Nevertheless, McAuley and colleagues observed, including fusion in decompression procedures is now common practice in some countries, particularly the U.S. and Australia. One analysis in 2023 found that fully 90% of U.S. surgeries for degenerative spondylolisthesis in 2019 involved spine fusion -- a 23-point increase from just 3 years previously. McAuley's group had no explanation for this explosion in popularity, while the authors of the 2023 analysis pointed to "financial incentives, lack of guidelines and/or national regulations, and delayed evidence dissemination through medical education or professional societies."

Degenerative spondylolisthesis is a common feature of spinal stenosis; it involves a forward shift in a vertebra relative to those below it. Some surgeons have viewed this as indicative of instability that should be rectified via fusion, which seems plausible on its face but, as noted above, rigorous evidence for actual benefit is weak at best.

The current study sought to extend the findings from that Norwegian trial, called NORDSTEN-DS, by examining spinal stenosis patients' outcomes as recorded in the country's national health registry. They identified a total of some 3,900 patients undergoing surgery for degenerative spondylolisthesis from 2007 to 2021. NORDSTEN-DS participants' data were included in the registry and analyzed anew in the current study, which used a "target trial emulation" approach to compare patients undergoing versus not having fusion as part of decompression surgery. After excluding patients who, for example, were very elderly or had previous surgeries in the same spinal region, the investigators had 2,252 patients for detailed analysis, including 236 who were in NORDSTEN-DS.

Mean patient age was about 65 and roughly 70% were women. ODI scores at the time of surgery averaged 38.9 for those having decompression alone and 41.4 for the group undergoing fusion (higher scores indicate worse symptoms, and the maximum is 50).

At month 12 after surgery, mean ODI scores declined to 20.0 for the fusion group and 22.3 among those undergoing decompression alone. The mean difference of 2.2 points fell short of statistical significance (95% CI -1.6 to 6.1).

McAuley and colleagues also performed some subgroup analyses to see whether patients who would be more likely to benefit from fusion could be identified from baseline characteristics, such as age, sex, body mass index, or symptom severity. This effort came up empty, as no significant differences in ODI improvement emerged. However, it did show that men with obesity (BMI ≥30) had significantly worse outcomes versus men with lower BMI values.

And, as with earlier studies, fusion led to longer operative time (mean 85 extra minutes) and longer hospital stays (mean 1.9 extra days) compared with decompression alone. Although no particular complication stood out as more common with fusion, the risk for any type of complication was doubled overall. Risk for needing additional surgery because of complications was increased even more.

"This study calls into question the highly prevalent management of pain from lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis with fusion," McAuley and colleagues wrote. "Our findings add to current evidence and should prompt reevaluation of current guidelines," which, they noted, are sparse and "offer conflicting recommendations."

Limitations to the study included the reliance on administrative records, the potential for confounding by unmeasured variables, and the 12-month window for examining outcomes, leaving open the possibility that fusion could have longer-term benefits.

#5820. Germany’s Hydrogen Pipeline Reached Marl. Its Market Still Needs to Add Up.

Germany’s hydrogen backbone achieved a genuine milestone on August 4, 2026. RWE and its partners announced that renewable hydrogen produced during commissioning at Lingen had reached Marl Chemical Park, roughly 120 kilometres away. Electrolysers, converted natural gas pipelines and industrial receiving infrastructure were working together.

The GET H2 consortium deserves credit for getting the equipment operating. But completing a hydrogen pipeline and establishing an economically competitive market for the hydrogen moving through it are different achievements.

The announcement did not disclose the quantity received at Marl, the price paid by an industrial customer or which existing hydrogen production was displaced. The English release describes hydrogen being available for industrial use, while the German release says it was used. Neither provides the industrial mass balance needed to determine the actual emissions benefit. The network also contained hydrogen from earlier commissioning activities, which makes tracing individual molecules through the pipeline less useful than measuring what changed at the receiving industrial facilities.

Marl is hardly a new hydrogen customer. The chemical park has used hydrogen for decades in integrated production processes. Providing another source may be useful, especially where renewable hydrogen replaces fossil-derived supply, but existing demand does not automatically become commercially viable demand for a considerably more expensive feedstock.

The larger infrastructure ambition makes that distinction important. Germany’s approved hydrogen core network covers 9,040 kilometres and has expected investment costs of €18.9 billion. Much of the network will use converted natural gas pipelines. These are approved plans and anticipated investments, not evidence that the entire network has been built or that future customers have committed to using it.

There are genuine industrial commitments. RWE has a 15-year agreement with TotalEnergies to supply approximately 30,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually to the Leuna refinery from 2030. That provides a named customer, volume and contract period. The price is undisclosed, and European fuel regulations help create demand for renewable hydrogen in refining.

That is a much stronger commercial signal than commissioning a pipeline. The question is how many comparable customers exist, what they can afford and whether their businesses will continue using hydrogen over the decades required to recover infrastructure investments.

The wider European outlook has become less optimistic. ENTSOG’s October 2026 draft assessment reduced its 2030 hydrogen demand assumption from 620 TWh to 335 TWh, a 46% reduction from its 2024 assessment. Its 2040 assumption fell 33%, from 1,929 TWh to 1,296 TWh. These are changes to European planning scenarios, not measurements of declining actual hydrogen consumption, but they matter when infrastructure economics depend on demand growth.

My central model of hydrogen supplied through the Lingen system produces an illustrative delivered cost of about €9.06/kg after assumed capital support, compared with a €3/kg conventional hydrogen benchmark. Those are scenario values, not RWE’s actual costs or the undisclosed price paid at Marl. The gap illustrates the challenge facing industrial manufacturers selling chemicals into competitive international markets.

Hydrogen remains an important industrial feedstock. Well-located connections between producers and customers with durable demand may be worthwhile. Germany needs evidence that the customers and products can support the investment, rather than assuming that building enough pipelines will bring the market into existence.

#5819. The Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Is Exactly What Harley Needs

It's finally happening: Harley-Davidson is bringing a proper Harley-looking beginner bike to the United States. Not some weird half-baked attempt like the Street line, but a proper Harley-styled cruiser that just happens to be built around a smaller, beginner-friendly engine. The new bike is called the Sprint 440, it's debuting at EICMA, and I couldn't be more excited for it.

I've long said that Harley needs a proper beginner bike, a way into the brand that capitalizes on what Milwaukee does well — vintage, call it "authentic" styling — without the company's usual high prices and general skull-themed accessorizing. The Sprint 440 appears to be just that: A practical single cylinder, a Sportster-esque sloped tank, and a price that lets beginners actually cross-shop Harley with Kawasaki and Triumph. While we don't know the firm U.S. price yet, we know the bike goes for just $8,500 Canadian up north — the equivalent of just over $6,000 here.

The Sprint looks leagues better than the Nightster it displaces as Harley's cheapest bike, with styling that better hides the brake lines, wires, and radiators a modern motorcycle requires. The Sprint could be mistaken for an Iron 883 by those who don't know the ins and outs of both bikes, though it does need some indicators of its foreign coproduction — the bike is a collaboration with India's Hero MotoCorp, according to RideApart, and its chain drive demonstrates that things aren't all Harley here. Still, it's a Milwaukee bike in the ways that really matter: Despite the foreign assistance, Harley says the bike will undergo final production in Pennsylvania.

Harley hasn't yet released all the specs for the U.S. model of the Sprint, but we know the international model has a 26.4-inch seat height (though Harley specifies that's "laden") and a 412-pound weight. Horsepower is low, at just 27, though it makes a full 28 pound-feet of torque. Those numbers aren't incredibly impressive, but if you're a new rider into the looks of a classic Harley you probably won't mind — you'll just appreciate a lighter, cheaper way to get the bike you want. That kind of accessibility is what Harley has been lacking for years, and I truly hope the Sprint 440 helps the brand get some new buyers in.
