#5764. Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover

For tens of millions of people, dental implants have provided a way to replace missing teeth with a full set of fixed, functional teeth rather than removable dentures. However, an estimated 10% to 20% of implant patients eventually develop peri-implantitis, a serious infection that damages the surrounding jawbone.

Antibiotics frequently fail to control this condition, and scientists have struggled to understand why. Now, researchers believe they have uncovered the mechanism responsible.

A new study published in PNAS Nexus by scientists at the Rutgers School of Dental Medicine reveals that bacteria can gradually corrode dental implants, releasing microscopic titanium particles into nearby tissues. These particles interfere with the immune cells responsible for fighting infection, trapping them in a state of excessive inflammation that progressively destroys jawbone.

The researchers examined human tissue samples, studied human immune cells in the laboratory, and conducted experiments using genetically engineered mice. Their investigation identified a calcium channel in macrophages, the immune cells that engulf bacteria, that becomes activated by titanium particles. When this channel was disabled in mice, the disease was prevented.

This discovery provides the first credible drug target for a condition that affects as many as one in five dental implant recipients and costs healthcare systems worldwide more than $1 billion annually.

"For the first time, we show why all the antibiotic treatments that work around teeth do not work around implants," said Georgios Kotsakis, senior author of the study and assistant dean for clinical research at Rutgers School of Dental Medicine. "Now that we know the cause, we can start developing therapeutics."

Why Dental Implant Infections Resist Antibiotics

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding peri-implantitis has been its similarity to periodontitis, the gum disease that develops around natural teeth. Both conditions begin with the same types of bacteria found in the mouth, yet they respond very differently to treatment.

For natural teeth, antibiotics combined with routine professional cleaning can resolve the infection. Around dental implants, however, the same medications are successful in fewer than half of cases. Even when treatment is attempted, the underlying jawbone may continue to deteriorate.

For the past two decades, scientists have largely concentrated on the bacteria responsible for these infections. Researchers in Kotsakis' laboratory decided to investigate another possible contributor: the implant material itself.

Their work showed that bacteria accumulating on implant surfaces create acidic biofilms that slowly damage the titanium. Over time, this corrosion can release billions of microscopic metal particles, each smaller than a red blood cell.

Titanium particles can also be dislodged during routine dental cleaning. This is particularly concerning when instruments designed for natural teeth are used on implants, because they can scrape and damage the metal surface.

How Titanium Particles Hijack the Immune System

Once released into the gums, the tiny titanium fragments attract a bacterial toxin known as lipopolysaccharide, which coats their surfaces. This combination creates a deceptive target for the immune system, making the particles resemble unusually large bacteria that cannot be broken down.

Macrophages, the white blood cells responsible for engulfing and destroying harmful microorganisms, attempt to consume these particles. But because the cells cannot digest titanium, they become stuck in a prolonged state of excessive inflammation.

As a result, the macrophages produce large quantities of inflammatory signaling molecules, including interleukin-1 beta. This protein is also associated with inflammatory processes involved in rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.

The resulting immune response gradually breaks down the bone supporting the dental implant. At the same time, the macrophages become less effective at fighting the bacteria that triggered the infection in the first place.

Laboratory experiments revealed just how severely their defenses were disrupted. Macrophages exposed to titanium particles engulfed fewer than half as many bacteria as immune cells that had not encountered the particles.

"These particles are little magnets that attract the bacterial toxin, and they hijack the immune system, preventing it from clearing bacteria," said Kotsakis. "You have a perfect storm that defies antibiotics."

Scientists Identify a Potential New Treatment Target

After uncovering how titanium particles disrupt immune defenses, the researchers investigated the molecular pathway responsible for the damaging reaction.

They traced the process to TRPC1, a calcium channel (a specialized, pore-forming protein structure within cell membranes) found in macrophages. This channel plays a central role in the inflammatory response triggered by titanium particles and bacterial toxins.

To test its importance, the team used genetically engineered mice that lacked TRPC1. When these animals were exposed to the same combination of titanium particles and bacteria, their immune systems responded much more effectively.

The mice developed dramatically smaller abscesses, produced fewer inflammatory signaling molecules, and regained the ability to clear bacteria. Disabling the channel prevented the destructive disease process observed when TRPC1 was present.

The results point toward a potentially new approach to treating peri-implantitis by targeting the immune system response rather than relying exclusively on antibiotics.

With funding from the National Institutes of Health, Kotsakis and his colleagues are now evaluating potential drugs that act on the same molecular pathway in human cells.

Why Proper Dental Implant Cleaning Matters

Although the research opens the door to future therapies, it also reinforces an important preventive measure for people who already have dental implants.

Regular professional cleaning remains the strongest known protection against peri-implantitis. However, the instruments and techniques used during those appointments can make a significant difference.

Until approximately a decade ago, many dentists routinely cleaned implants with the same metal scalers used to remove deposits from natural teeth. Research by the Rutgers team and other scientists has since demonstrated that these tools can damage and corrode titanium surfaces, potentially releasing additional particles and accelerating the disease.

Today, nonabrasive cleaning methods have become standard practice, helping protect implant surfaces while reducing the risk of complications.

By revealing how corroded titanium can interfere with immune defenses, the findings offer a new explanation for why some dental implant infections are so difficult to treat and identify a promising direction for developing more effective therapies.

#5763. Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds

Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Alignment Healthcare is lowering its guidance for the year as it faces significant headwinds to finish out 2026.

The company said in an earnings report released late Thursday that it now expects to bring in $100 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, as well as $5.2 billion in revenue. Total membership is set to be at least 305,000, according to the report.

Alignment reported an $8 million loss in the third quarter, compared to a $3.8 million profit one year ago. Profits were $39.9 million through three quarters, up from $10.3 million across the first nine months of 2025.

Revenue in the third quarter was $1.4 billion, compared to $663.7 million in the prior-year quarter. Revenues through the first nine months of 2026 were $3.9 billion, up from $2.9 billion through three quarters in 2025.

CEO John Kao told investors on the company's earnings call Friday morning that some headwinds Alignment is facing include cost spikes in certain service lines, like catastrophic care and skilled nursing, as well as volatility in claims processing.

Last year, Alignment kicked off an effort to migrate to a comprehensive claims system with the goal of accelerating payment speed, growing automated adjudication rates and enhancing payment integrity. Through that process, once the dust settled on the shift, Alignment found "a notable increase in aggressive provider appeal and disputes in our paid claims data" that also drove up costs, Kao said.

Kao said that the insurer has spent the last several months building out its payment integrity capabilities, as well as deploying additional resources to support clinical best practices to mitigate the variation in outcomes for members.

He said that these investments have driven improvements, particularly in September and into October, but the company is still taking a cautious approach to the end of the year.

"Despite our progress, we are taking a prudent approach to the increased trend seen in Q3 and assume that higher costs in the third quarter will continue to weigh on our results for the remainder of the year," Kao said. "I want to emphasize that the guidance we have provided today is a guidance that we are confident in delivering."

Kao also addressed Alignment's performance in the latest round of star ratings scores. Based on federal data, 25% of its members are in plans with at least four stars in 2027, down from 100% in 2026. That four-star threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments in Medicare Advantage.

He said that six of the company's seven contracts were above four stars, but a 3.5 score on the remaining plan, a core HMO offering in California, dragged down its overall performance.

Kao said that the team is "focused on really getting to the root issues in Stars." Alignment has also sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services over the 2027 calculations.

"That's something that we're going to be underscoring yet again," he said. "This is something that everybody in the company has to focus on ... and we'll get this fixed."

#5762. Honda Is Building A Racier Civic Type R For The U.S.

Toyota has the new, rear-seat-less GRMN Corolla, Hyundai has its big-winged Elantra N TCR, and soon Honda will be bringing an even nuttier version of its Civic Type R to the party. On Friday, Honda confirmed that a Honda Racing Corporation version of its high-performance hatchback "is in development for the U.S. market." Translation: Honda is working on an even racier Civic Type R to sell in America. The company first showed off that HRC Concept at the Tokyo Auto Salon back in January, but it landed in North America for the first time at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas last week.

Not much is known about the HRC Civic, but judging from the red-and-purple-camo'd Concept, expect it to get more aggressive aero parts and cooling. If we had to guess based on how this sort of thing tends to go, we'd put our money on different, lighter wheels, stickier tires, tweaked suspension parts, some chassis stiffening, and maybe a modest power bump. Although we also wouldn't be that surprised if it doesn't come with any more power than the 315-hp standard model.

Honda says the CTR HRC is being made in the name of "ultimate pure sports performance" using HRC tech and racing driver expertise. A more extreme driving experience, then, is a given, but those specific words also read to us as "less compromising as a daily driver." Not unexpected or entirely a bad thing, given the premise, but probably not the Type R to get if you plan to, say, daily it year-round.

In any case, the HRC Concept CTR isn't the only car at Honda's SEMA stand this year, as it's joined by a Passport Baja trophy truck, a Passport TrailSport Baja Chase support vehicle, a Prelude modified by Hasport, and a handful of the automaker's race cars, including this year's Aston Martin AMR26 Formula 1 car, which uses a Honda RA626H power unit. Hopefully, the pumped-up Civic Type R that'll eventually hit U.S. showrooms will be a lot more competitive than that Aston.

#5760. Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues

Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sutter Health scrapped plans to build a flagship campus on property it owns in Emeryville, California, and instead is shifting its focus to outpatient care in the area, according to a Sept. 30 statement.

The health system announced those plans in early 2025 (see that story below), with a medical center of up to 200 beds as the centerpiece of a $1 billion investment into San Francisco's East Bay. It attributed its decision to "the lack of a clear and predictable regulatory path" related to California environmental and land use law.

"Over two years, we pursued relief under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA," the statement reads. "Those efforts did not secure the certainty needed to advance the hospital project, leaving it vulnerable to litigation that could delay construction and new hospital services for years."

Accompanying plans surrounding outpatient services "including primary and specialty care, diagnostic services and outpatient surgery" are now the priority for that community, though Sutter said it's still keeping an eye out for another potential location for a future hospital.

"Separating these projects keeps healthcare investment moving and allows us to advance additional outpatient services that can bring care to patients sooner. No alternative location has been selected, and we are assessing several options that can support comprehensive hospital, emergency and specialty care and the infrastructure needed for the future."

Sutter said that services will not be affected at Alta Bates, another hospital in the area it was planning to relieve with the new build, and that it plans to keep supporting that campus until another hospital can be finished. It added that hospitals across California have and continue to face "legal and regulatory challenges [tied to] significant seismic deadlines, while efforts to modernize or replace facilities can be exposed to lengthy regulatory reviews and litigation. A different location alone will not resolve these challenges."

Sutter Health will invest $1 billion to expand its services across Northern California's East Bay region, including a new flagship campus in Emeryville.

The health system announced Wednesday that the campus will feature a new medical center with up to 200 beds as well as a regional destination for ambulatory care. The plans also leave room for future expansion, according to the announcement.

The ambulatory services complex at the 12-acre campus will feature a wide array of specialties and will offer imaging and laboratory services. It expects to welcome its first patients as early as 2028, Sutter said.

The 335,000-square-foot medical center will include labor and delivery, surgical services, intensive care, emergency care and neonatal intensive care. The facility will be designed with the potential to add additional patient rooms in the future.

Sutter is targeting a 2032-33 opening date for the medical center, according to the announcement.

“Our Emeryville campus project represents one of the most significant investments we’re making across our system over the next decade and is part of our broader vision to meet the community’s growing demand for expanded access to our services across the East Bay footprint,” said Warner Thomas, president and CEO of Sutter Health, in the press release.

Sutter said it will put a focus on recruiting both primary care physicians and specialty care doctors, breaking down patient barriers to appointments and referrals and investing in initiatives to bolster the healthcare workforce. It expects to have 190 primary and specialty care clinicians staffing the new campus.

Beyond building the new campus, Sutter said it plans to grow the behavioral health services offered at its Herrick campus in Berkeley. The health system's Alta Bates campus will continue to operate as an acute care facility until the new medical center opens in Emeryville and then will be overhauled to provide ambulatory surgery services, urgent care and potentially skilled nursing services.

The health system is also renovating a medical office building in Berkley to serve as a primary care facility that will also offer OB-GYN care, according to the announcement.

Additional renovations are in the works as well, Sutter said.

“Too many people face challenges in accessing the care they need," Thomas said. "At Sutter, we’re committed to breaking down those barriers—expanding care facilities, enhancing imaging capabilities, improving online appointment scheduling and collaborating with the Sutter East Bay Medical Group and our community physician partners to attract more primary and specialty care physicians.

"These efforts will allow us to care for more patients while also investing in programs and partnerships that build the healthcare workforce of the future—ensuring more people get the right care when and where they need it," he said.

#5759. Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells

Scientists have identified a remarkable protein switch that influences whether cells burn fat or store it. Disabling this protein increases fat consumption and interferes with the formation of new fat cells, raising the possibility of a different approach to treating obesity. Subsequent research has strengthened the discovery, revealing that the same protein helps regulate how much energy the body burns.

What if one of the keys to fighting obesity lies not in suppressing appetite, but in changing how the body's cells use energy?

Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science have identified a protein called MTCH2, nicknamed "Mitch," that plays an important role in controlling metabolism. When scientists disabled this protein in laboratory experiments, cells began consuming more fuel, including fats and carbohydrates. They also found that removing Mitch could interfere with the process through which immature cells develop into fat cells.

The discovery builds on earlier experiments in mice, in which switching off Mitch in muscle tissue increased energy expenditure, improved endurance, and protected the animals from diet-related obesity.

The findings, published in The EMBO Journal in January 2025, suggest that manipulating this protein could eventually offer a way to influence both fat burning and fat accumulation. Additional research published later that year has provided further evidence of its importance in regulating body fat and metabolism.

Why Scientists Are Searching for Better Obesity Treatments

Over the past decade, medications designed to promote weight loss have transformed obesity treatment. Drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide have helped many patients achieve substantial reductions in body weight, largely by influencing appetite and the body's responses to food.

But losing weight does not necessarily mean losing only fat.

Weight reduction can also involve a decline in lean body mass, which includes muscle and other tissues. Preserving muscle is especially important because it supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

A 2026 analysis of 20 clinical trials involving 15,782 participants found that lean mass accounted for approximately 25% to 39% of the weight lost with several widely used weight-loss medications. Importantly, the researchers found that comparable proportional losses also occurred with lifestyle interventions, while adding resistance training helped preserve more lean tissue.

These concerns have encouraged scientists to investigate ways to reduce body fat while protecting the muscles needed for long-term health.

Professor Atan Gross and his colleagues at the Weizmann Institute arrived at a possible avenue through an unexpected discovery involving Mitch.

Switching Off One Protein Protected Mice From Obesity

In earlier experiments, Gross's team reduced the activity of MTCH2 in the muscles of mice. The effects were striking.

The genetically modified animals showed increased metabolic activity and were resistant to obesity caused by their diet. Their muscles also developed more fibers with a high capacity for using oxygen, helping improve physical endurance.

The mice performed better in exercise and stress tests and showed improvements in heart function. In addition to resisting excess fat accumulation, they experienced favorable changes in their overall body composition.

The results suggested that Mitch was doing much more than controlling a single metabolic reaction. Somehow, this protein appeared to influence the body's ability to use energy, store fat, and sustain physical activity.

That raised an intriguing question: How could disabling one protein produce such widespread effects?

To investigate, the researchers turned their attention to mitochondria, the microscopic structures responsible for supplying much of the energy that cells need to function.

The Mitochondria Connection Behind Fat Burning

Mitochondria are frequently described as the powerhouses of cells because they convert energy from food into a usable form called ATP, or adenosine triphosphate.

ATP acts as a cellular energy currency. Muscles use it to contract, cells need it to grow and repair themselves, and countless biological processes depend on a steady supply.

However, mitochondria are not static structures. They constantly change shape, joining together into larger networks or separating into smaller units.

When mitochondria fuse, they can form interconnected systems that help coordinate energy production. When they divide, the resulting structures may operate differently, altering how efficiently cells produce and consume energy.

Gross's team had previously established that Mitch plays a major role in mitochondrial fusion, the process that allows separate mitochondria to merge.

Without this protein, the mitochondrial network becomes fragmented. Although the cells can still generate energy, they experience changes in energy efficiency and demand that can force them to consume more fuel.

This offered a possible explanation for the unusual metabolism observed in the mice. Instead of conserving energy efficiently, their cells appeared to be operating in a more energy-intensive state.

But would disabling Mitch have a similar effect in human cells?

Human Cells Begin Burning More Fat Without Mitch

To answer that question, researchers led by doctoral student Sabita Chourasia used genetic engineering to remove MTCH2 from human cells grown in the laboratory.

The change disrupted the normal structure of their mitochondrial networks. Individual mitochondria became more separated, and the balance between energy production and energy demand shifted.

The cells developed a persistent shortage of readily available energy relative to their needs, even as their mitochondria increased their oxygen-consuming activity.

To compensate, they began consuming more nutrients.

"After deleting Mitch, we examined, every few hours, the effect that had on more than 100 substances taking part in metabolism in human cells," Chourasia explains. "We saw an increase in cellular respiration, the process in which the cell produces energy from nutrients, such as carbohydrates and fats, using oxygen. This explains the increase in muscular endurance in previous experiments using mice."

Cellular respiration is the series of chemical reactions that allows cells to extract usable energy from nutrients. Increasing this activity generally requires a greater supply of fuel.

The researchers found that cells lacking Mitch consumed more fats, carbohydrates, and amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

Fat metabolism was particularly revealing.

Rather than relying on their usual mix of energy sources, the altered cells increased their use of fatty acids for fuel. This indicated that MTCH2 influences not only how much energy cells consume, but also which nutrients they use to meet that demand.

"We discovered that deleting Mitch led to a major drop in fats in membranes," Gross explains. "At the same time, we saw an increase in fatty substances used to produce energy, and we realized that the fat was being broken down from the membrane to be used as fuel. In other words, we showed that Mitch determines the fate of fat in human cells."

Cell membranes are thin, flexible barriers made largely from fatty molecules called lipids. They protect cells and organize many of their essential functions.

The findings suggested that cells deprived of Mitch were changing how they distributed and used these lipids, drawing on some of their available fatty resources to support increased energy consumption.

Detailed analysis also revealed changes in stored lipids, demonstrating that the effect was more complex than simply eliminating cellular fat. Overall, the results showed that MTCH2 is a powerful regulator of how cells allocate nutrients between energy production and other biological needs.

The researchers then investigated whether Mitch also influences how fat cells develop.

This question was particularly interesting because previous studies had found elevated MTCH2 levels in fat tissue from women with obesity.

Fat cells, also known as adipocytes, do not appear fully formed. They develop from immature precursor cells through a process called adipogenesis, or fat cell differentiation.

As these precursor cells mature, they must build new cellular structures, produce fats, and activate genes that allow them to specialize in storing energy.

All of this requires considerable energy and raw materials.

Gross's team suspected that removing Mitch might disrupt the process by creating an environment in which cells were too busy consuming fuel to build the components needed for fat storage.

Experiments using mouse precursor fat cells supported this idea. When the researchers deleted MTCH2, far fewer cells successfully developed into mature fat cells.

In the published experiments, approximately 80% to 90% of normal precursor cells differentiated within six days, compared with only 5% to 10% of cells lacking MTCH2. The altered cells also accumulated substantially fewer lipid droplets, the structures used to store fat.

"When we deleted Mitch from the progenitor cells, we discovered that the environment created in these cells was not conducive to the synthesis of new fats," Gross explains. "Reducing the ability to synthesize membranes prevents the cells from growing, developing and reaching the point where differentiation is possible. The process of fat accumulation requires a large amount of available energy, but in cells without Mitch, there is a shortage of energy. In addition, the expression of genes necessary for differentiation is suppressed, and there is a shortage of the substances vital for this process to occur. As a result, differentiation of new fat cells is reduced, along with fat accumulation."

In other words, disabling Mitch appeared to affect fat metabolism in two distinct ways. It increased the consumption of energy-rich nutrients and interfered with the cellular machinery needed to develop new fat-storing cells.

Importantly, the fat cell differentiation experiments used a mouse-derived cell line, while the detailed analysis of nutrient consumption was conducted in human cells. The combined results suggest a broader role for the protein, but they do not establish that blocking MTCH2 would prevent new fat cells from forming in people.

Follow-Up Research Reveals Another Fat-Burning Mechanism

The importance of MTCH2 became even clearer in research published on October 3, 2025, in Nature Communications.

An international research team, which included Gross and Chourasia, investigated how MTCH2 influences metabolism in fat tissue. By analyzing human and mouse fat samples, studying cultured fat cells, and conducting experiments in genetically modified mice, the scientists identified another mechanism linking this protein to energy expenditure.

They found that MTCH2 helps regulate the movement of fatty acids into mitochondria, where these molecules can be broken down to produce energy.

The process involves an enzyme called carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1, or CPT1. This enzyme acts as an important checkpoint, helping determine how much fat can enter mitochondria for use as fuel.

Normally, CPT1 activity is regulated by a molecule called malonyl-CoA, which signals when cells should limit fatty acid consumption.

The researchers discovered that MTCH2 physically interacts with CPT1 and influences how strongly this regulatory signal affects the enzyme.

Removing MTCH2 altered that control system, allowing mitochondria to increase fatty acid utilization and energy expenditure.

This provided a more detailed molecular explanation for why disabling the protein could encourage cells to burn additional fat.

Mice Burned More Energy Without Eating Less

The follow-up study also produced an especially promising result.

When researchers removed MTCH2 specifically from the fat cells of mice, the animals burned more energy without increasing their physical activity or changing how much food they consumed.

Under a regular diet, the genetically modified mice gained weight at a rate similar to that of normal mice.

However, when the animals were fed a high-fat diet, a difference emerged.

Mice lacking MTCH2 in their fat tissue gained less weight and accumulated less body fat than untreated mice, despite consuming similar amounts of food.

Their lean body mass remained comparable to that of the control animals.

The genetically modified mice also demonstrated improved glucose tolerance, indicating that their bodies were better able to manage blood sugar after receiving glucose. In addition, their cholesterol levels were lower.

These findings strengthened the evidence that MTCH2 influences whole-body metabolism, rather than simply changing the behavior of isolated cells.

The scientists also found that its metabolic effects could occur independently of UCP1, a protein commonly associated with heat production in brown fat. Brown fat is a specialized form of body fat that helps generate heat by burning energy, whereas white fat primarily stores excess energy.

Discovering an additional pathway for increasing energy expenditure could be important because it offers researchers another potential target for treating obesity and related metabolic disorders.

Could This Protein Lead to Better Weight-Loss Treatments?

Together, the findings suggest that MTCH2 may be an important molecular switch linking fat storage, energy consumption, and the development of fat cells.

The original experiments showed that removing the protein could increase nutrient consumption in human cells and interfere with fat cell formation in mouse cells. The later research demonstrated that selectively removing MTCH2 from fat tissue could increase energy expenditure and protect mice against excessive weight gain on a high-fat diet.

That combination raises the possibility of developing treatments that change how the body handles energy, potentially complementing medications that primarily work by reducing appetite.

However, several major questions remain unanswered.

Scientists have not yet demonstrated that inhibiting MTCH2 produces safe, sustained weight loss in humans. The protein also participates in other important biological activities, including mitochondrial regulation and pathways involved in cell survival. Blocking it throughout the body could therefore produce unwanted consequences.

Preventing fat cells from forming is not necessarily beneficial in every situation, either. Healthy fat tissue plays an essential role in storing excess energy, maintaining blood sugar balance, and producing hormones. Disrupting its function could potentially redirect fats into organs where they may cause harm.

Researchers will need to determine whether MTCH2 can be targeted safely, which tissues would benefit most, and whether reducing its activity would preserve muscle health while promoting fat loss.

For now, established strategies such as resistance exercise and adequate protein intake remain important for protecting muscle during weight reduction. A 2026 review of clinical trials found that combining lifestyle changes with resistance training produced a more favorable pattern of lean mass preservation than weight-loss interventions without such exercise.

The research nevertheless points toward a compelling possibility: Rather than focusing exclusively on how much food the body takes in, future obesity treatments might also influence how cells decide whether to burn energy or store it.

And one protein, Mitch, appears to be deeply involved in that decision.

The original study, titled "MTCH2 controls energy demand and expenditure to fuel anabolism during adipogenesis," was published in The EMBO Journal on January 3, 2025.

The research was led by Sabita Chourasia and Professor Atan Gross at the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Additional contributors included Dr. Christopher Petucci, Clarissa Shoffler, and Dina Abbasian from the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia; Hu Wang and Professor Xianlin Han from the University of Texas at San Antonio; Dr. Ehud Sivan, Dr. Alexander Brandis, Tevie Mehlman, Dr. Sergey Malitsky, Dr. Maxim Itkin, Dr. Ayala Sharp, Dr. Ron Rotkopf, and Dr. Bareket Dassa from Weizmann's Life Sciences Core Facilities Department; and Dr. Limor Regev and Dr. Yehudit Zaltsman from Weizmann's Immunology and Regenerative Biology Department.

The follow-up study, "MTCH2 modulates CPT1 activity to regulate lipid metabolism of adipocytes," was published in Nature Communications on October 3, 2025. It involved an international collaboration, including researchers affiliated with ETH Zurich, Weizmann Institute of Science, and other institutions.

Materials provided by Weizmann Institute of Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5758. Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds

Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Oct. 26 to 30.

Doximity launched DoseCheck, a new safety feature within Doximity Ask designed to catch unsafe or incorrect medication dosing recommendations generated by artificial intelligence.

Doximity Ask is the company's clinical decision support tool.

Rather than relying on an LLM to double-check another LLM, DoseCheck adds a deterministic, rule-based verification layer, checking AI-generated dosing claims against structured information including FDA labeling and professional guidelines, the company said. By checking against FDA labeling and professional guidelines, DoseCheck increases accuracy to more than 99%, the company claims.

Doximity tested nine widely used AI models with over 8,000 dosing questions based on real physician queries. At least 2.3% of dosing claims made by these models were wrong, and 43.8% of detected errors were serious or potentially lethal.

According to the analysis, common sources of errors include dosing newer drugs, failing to account for patient-specific factors such as kidney function, age, weight and medical history, and mistakes involving units, decimal points or drugs with similar names.

"AI is probabilistic. Drug dosing can’t be," said Louis-Antoine Mullie, M.D., chief AI researcher at Doximity. "DoseCheck doesn’t ask a language model to grade its own homework. It checks dosing claims against a structured, authoritative database, so physicians get the same verified dosing answer every time."

DoseCheck is free and has been rolled out to all Doximity Ask users across mobile and desktop.

Health and wellness platform Hims & Hers plans to launch a peptides specialty after the federal government signaled it will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture six peptides temporarily.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services will not take action against licensed pharmacists who dispense certain unapproved peptides, according to a new policy published this week in the Federal Register.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Through its new Peptides+ specialty, Hims & Hers plans to offer access to Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable. "If a customer is eligible, a personalized treatment plan will be prescribed and delivered by independent providers, treatments supplied by licensed pharmacies, with ongoing clinical support our customers can trust," CEO Andrew Dudum wrote in a blog post.

"We’re focused on entering this specialty the right way, not the fastest. Most of what we know about these compounds is still early—with limited published studies, we draw primarily from clinical experience from the last decade. We’ve consistently acknowledged that while these compounds hold promise, there is still information we do not yet know. Provider-supervised use is how we plan to build on this foundation and make sure that access and innovation can move at the same pace," Dudum said.

The tech giant launched Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate, a new program designed to teach healthcare professionals responsible, practical ways to use AI in their day-to-day work. Clinicians at Google developed the virtual course, and the program is accredited for up to five American Medical Association (AMA) continuing education credits.

The NYU Grossman School of Medicine, the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Touro University are offering the program to their faculty, residents and medical students. Leading nursing institutions, including Purdue University School of Nursing, are offering the certificate as part of their healthcare professional training, according to Google.

"As I’ve traveled around the world this year, I’ve heard loud and clear from healthcare professionals how much need there is for a thoughtful but practical educational resource on AI, made specifically for healthcare," Michael Howell, M.D., Google’s chief health officer, wrote in a blog post.

Large language models recommend more up-front testing, referrals and treatment than the physicians who actually saw the patients and at more than three times the cost, according to a study published in NEJM AI.

Researchers from the Technion, Stanford University and collaborating institutions tested 20 general-purpose and four specialized medical AI systems on records from 200 real outpatient and emergency visits. Each received the clinical presentation without the physician’s assessment and plan. The team priced the recommended tests and referrals in both the AI and physicians’ plans using the same 2026 Medicare rates.

Across the 20 general-purpose systems, AI-suggested care cost a mean of $314 per visit, compared with $97 for care recommended by attending physicians. Suggested care was more costly in 180 of 200 cases. The average cost of care per AI system ranged from $209 to $599.

Diagnostic testing rose from $71 per visit in the physicians’ plans to $176 across the systems, about $105 more per visit. The referral rates for the physician’s plans were 0.15 per visit compared to 0.87 for the LLM’s plans, which, at the corresponding Medicare rates, is $111 more per visit, according to the study.

"The four specialized medical systems showed comparable excess (2.7× to 3.5×), so medical fine-tuning did not curb—and may reinforce—cost escalation," the study authors wrote.

The researchers used MTSamples, a publicly available collection of 4,999 real de-identified medical transcription sample reports contributed by practicing clinicians as reference material for medical transcriptionists. The notes are documentation from real patient visits, but they are a convenience sample assembled for transcription training rather than a representative draw from U.S. ambulatory practice, the study authors wrote.

"Under a single standard prompt, every AI system we evaluated, general purpose and medically specialized alike, suggested more diagnostic tests, medications and specialist referrals than the treating physician on the same cases," the study authors wrote.

LLMs appear optimized to be comprehensive and avoid missing diagnoses, and may show an analogous tendency toward exhaustive workup, the study authors noted.

The researchers argued that much of the excess can be reduced through better prompting, suggesting cost inflation is partly a deployment and design problem rather than an unavoidable feature of AI.

Researchers reevaluated 19 models using different instructions. A simple cost-aware prompt telling models to recommend only clinically necessary, cost-effective items reduced average recommended costs from 3.2 times physician costs to 2.5 times.

A stronger "parsimonious-but-safe" prompt told models to focus on the three most likely diagnoses, explicitly rule out dangerous "cannot-miss" conditions, and recommend only tests whose results would change management. That cut costs to just 1.4 times physician costs. But diagnostic agreement with physicians fell in 17 of the 19 systems, illustrating why cost reductions need to be evaluated alongside other changes in the recommendations, the study authors noted.

"Getting the diagnosis right matters, but so does the path you take to get there," said Prof. Dvir Aran of the Technion, the study’s corresponding author, in a statement. "Accuracy and safety have dominated how clinical AI is trained and evaluated. Efficiency needs the same attention: whether each test or referral is likely to help the patient."

Digital health company Eko Health launched a new stethoscope, the CORE 300, that integrates traditional and digital listening modes directly into a single chestpiece.

The AI-enabled stethoscope, which received FDA clearance, is also in line with premium traditional stethoscopes, making the digital technology more accessible to a broader group of healthcare professionals, the company said.

With a twist of the chestpiece, clinicians can switch between familiar traditional listening and Eko’s advanced digital listening technology, with up to 35x amplification, active noise cancellation and real-time heart rate displayed directly on the device. When connected to the Eko App and Eko's FDA-cleared AI for structural murmur detection, CORE 300 can also bring AI disease detection into the physical exam.

"Millions of healthcare professionals around the world use a stethoscope to examine patients every day," said Connor Landgraf, co-founder and CEO of Eko Health, in a statement. "Our goal is to bring the most ubiquitous clinical exam into the precise digital era. Once the physical exam becomes digital, we combine better listening with objective measurements and AI-powered clinical decision support right at the point of care."Clinical technologies are evolving quickly, but adoption depends on making new capabilities fit naturally into the way clinicians already practice, said Steven R. Steinhubl, M.D., chief medical officer of Eko Health and a board-certified cardiologist.

"CORE 300 bridges that gap. It preserves the traditional experience of auscultation while putting enhanced digital listening, objective measurements, and access to clinical decision support a twist of the chestpiece away. That combination can help make a smarter, more connected physical exam a routine part of care rather than the exception," Steinhubl said.

With Eko's digital stethoscope, clinicians can record, visualize and save heart, lung and body sounds and interpret the data with Eko’s FDA-cleared AI and software. According to the company, the device could expand screening capabilities in primary care offices, busy clinics and rural healthcare settings.

Eko Health launched its first Eko CORE digital stethoscope attachment in 2025, and to date, has delivered more than 750,000 digital stethoscopes and AI-enabled devices worldwide.

Healthcare engagement and payment solutions provider RevSpring debuted a conversational intelligent virtual agent that helps patients manage payment plans over the phone.

Let’s Talk expands on RevSpring’s voice platform and is integrated with its payment portal. It gives patients the ability to make payments, create payment plans, ask questions and respond to outbound voice reminders.

Initial results of the tool show a 36% increase in patient payment rates and a 27% decrease in transfer to live agents, the company says. Moreover, average call durations decreased 25% with Let’s Talk.

“Healthcare organizations are looking for ways to automate more patient interactions and improve financial outcomes without losing sight of the need for patient empathy,” said Scott MacKenzie, RevSpring CEO, in a statement. “Adding payment plans to Let’s Talk expands what patients can accomplish through conversational self-service, helping more callers resolve their needs without transferring to a representative. We’re building on years of proven payment automation to help providers improve efficiency and scale self-service across the patient financial experience.”

Enterprise healthcare operations software provider symplr launched Monday an integrated workforce management solution combining AI-driven scheduling and timekeeping.

The tool—dubbed symplr Time and Scheduling—combines symplr’s predictive nurse and staffing scheduling tool with its timekeeping solution. Nurse managers can identify and address staffing gaps "hundreds of days in advance," ultimately reducing time spent on staffing and timecard tasks by approximately 50%, executives say.

"Nurse leaders shouldn’t have to spend hours building schedules and scrambling to fill open shifts when they could be supporting their teams and patients," said Ali Morin, symplr chief nursing informatics officer, in a statement. "Nurses want more flexibility and predictability, while health systems need the right people in the right place at the right time. We designed symplr Time and Scheduling to deliver both, giving nurses and nurse leaders more time for patient care and less time managing the work around it."

Additional AI capabilities are expected to roll out in 2027, the company says.

Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute launched an AI task force Monday in a bid to evaluate the technologies and streamline adoption in a "safe and deliberate manner."

The task force is dubbed the Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy. It is led by Paul Thambi, M.D., and Louis Williams, M.D. AI is currently being used by the institute to personalize radiation doses, reduce note-taking time and streamline patient referral processes, according to the Oct. 27 announcement.

Williams said in a statement that it’s "crucial to have a system to continuously re-evaluate the effectiveness of each tool," adding that outputs of models should be analyzed on "an ongoing basis."

"There can be drift in a model that may influence its accuracy over time or there may be bias in the model that isn’t apparent upfront," Williams said. "That’s why it’s necessary to have a unified strategy that includes training models to identify mistakes before a model goes into production as well as longitudinal risk assessment to ensure safety."

#5757. Cool Temps and HF; Death After On-Field Collision; Shave and Shake in Stenting

— Recent developments of interest in cardiovascular medicine

A large nationwide study found an association between cooler ambient temperature and heart failure (HF) hospitalizations. (JAMA Network Open)

Energy drinks and stimulant supplements were frequently involved in cases of cardiac arrest and heart attack in young people, according to an FDA adverse event report analysis highlighted by the American Heart Association.

Abbott announced FDA approval for the Amplatzer Paraclose PVL Occluder, a transcatheter device for paravalvular leakage around a surgical heart valve.

The company also shared that the next-generation Amulet 360 Left Atrial Appendage Occluder had strong 1-year closure results.

A Spanish soccer player died in the hospital after having gone into cardiac arrest following an on-field collision. (AP)

An intervention to strengthen emergency dispatch and activate trained community responders was linked to increased bystander-initiated CPR before the arrival of emergency medical services for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, a cluster-randomized trial in France showed. (Lancet Public Health)

Heart muscle has the unique ability to burn glucose in the cytosol while simultaneously burning lactate in the mitochondria. (Nature)

In a randomized trial of people with severe pure aortic regurgitation, transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement reduced 1-year clinical events at the cost of more 30-day bleeding and new permanent pacemaker implantation. (Circulation)

The SIRONA trialists compared sirolimus- versus paclitaxel-coated balloons for femoropopliteal artery disease and found no major differences in walking function and quality of life, though clinically driven target lesion revascularization rates did favor the sirolimus group. (JACC: Cardiovascular Interventions)

Ten years into the DECISION-CTO trial, an initial percutaneous coronary intervention strategy for chronic total occlusion was not associated with a survival benefit. (Journal of the American College of Cardiology)

Mount Sinai operators achieved better stent placement among calcified coronary nodules if they employed both rotational atherectomy and lithotripsy to aid stent expansion, a so-called "Shave and Shake" strategy, the NODULE-SHOCK trial showed.

Among stroke patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, lower cervical curvature was associated with greater recanalization success, researchers found from a retrospective analysis. (Stroke)

In Dutch patients with angina and nonobstructive coronary arteries, coronary microvascular dysfunction apparently had no effect on clinical outcomes, registry data showed. (JAMA Cardiology)

Preterm infants tended to have worse survival with pharmacological therapy for patent ductus arteriosus, without any reduction in bronchopulmonary dysplasia, according to a meta-analysis. (Lancet Child & Adolescent Health)

#5756. Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain

A new study suggests that the Mediterranean diet may protect the heart, brain, and aging cells through a surprising biological mechanism involving tiny proteins produced by mitochondria, the structures responsible for generating most of the energy our cells need.

Researchers at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology discovered that people who more closely followed the Mediterranean diet had higher levels of two mitochondrial microproteins called humanin and SHMOOSE. Both have previously been linked to protection against cardiovascular disease and neurodegeneration, the gradual deterioration of nerve cells that occurs in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.

The study, led by USC Leonard Davis Instructional Associate Professor of Gerontology Roberto Vicinanza, offers a possible explanation for how everyday food choices influence cellular health and the aging process.

"These microproteins may act as molecular messengers that translate what we eat into how our cells function and age," Vicinanza said. "It's a new biological pathway that helps explain why the Mediterranean diet is so powerful."

How the Mediterranean Diet May Protect Aging Cells

The Mediterranean diet emphasizes foods such as olive oil, fish, beans, lentils, fruits, and vegetables. It has consistently been associated with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive decline. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly how this eating pattern produces its wide-ranging health benefits.

To investigate, the researchers examined blood samples from older adults who followed the Mediterranean diet to different degrees. Those whose eating habits most closely matched the diet had significantly higher concentrations of humanin and SHMOOSE.

They also showed lower indicators of oxidative stress, a process in which harmful molecules called reactive oxygen species overwhelm the body's protective defenses. Over time, oxidative stress can damage proteins, DNA, and other cellular components, contributing to aging and chronic disease.

Interestingly, the researchers found that certain foods were associated with different microproteins. Higher consumption of olive oil, fish, and legumes was linked to increased humanin levels. Meanwhile, olive oil consumption and eating fewer refined carbohydrates were associated with higher levels of SHMOOSE.

Refined carbohydrates include foods made with heavily processed grains and sugars, such as white bread, pastries, and many sugary snacks. These foods generally contain less fiber and fewer naturally occurring nutrients than their minimally processed counterparts.

"These findings suggest that specific components of the Mediterranean diet may directly influence mitochondrial biology," said USC Leonard Davis School Dean and USC Distinguished Professor Pinchas Cohen, the study's senior author. "Humanin and SHMOOSE could serve as biomarkers for adherence to the Mediterranean diet and have clinical significance."

Biomarkers are measurable biological indicators that can provide information about a person's health or physiological state. In this case, the researchers suggest that humanin and SHMOOSE could eventually help scientists understand how closely someone's diet aligns with healthy eating patterns and how their cells respond.

Tiny Mitochondrial Proteins With Powerful Effects

The findings extend a scientific effort spanning more than 20 years to investigate small proteins produced by mitochondria. Cohen has played a leading role in discovering and studying these molecules, which are increasingly recognized as important participants in cellular health.

Mitochondria are often described as the powerhouses of cells because they produce much of the energy required for essential biological activities. But their role extends beyond energy production. They also help regulate metabolism, cellular stress responses, and processes associated with aging.

Unlike most proteins, which are produced using instructions stored in the DNA inside the cell's nucleus, mitochondrial microproteins originate from genetic instructions within mitochondria themselves.

These instructions are found in small segments of mitochondrial DNA known as open reading frames. Some of these regions were once considered nonfunctional, but researchers have discovered that they can encode biologically active molecules.

One of the best understood is humanin, first identified by Cohen and fellow researchers in 2003. Subsequent studies have associated humanin with improved insulin sensitivity, better cardiovascular health, increased longevity, and protection of cognitive abilities.

Insulin sensitivity refers to how effectively the body's cells respond to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar. Maintaining healthy insulin sensitivity is important for metabolic health and reducing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Another intriguing microprotein is SHMOOSE (Small Human Mitochondrial ORF Over SErine tRNA), which was identified more recently by Cohen's research team.

SHMOOSE has attracted particular interest because of its possible role in protecting the brain. Scientists have found that a genetic variant of SHMOOSE is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. The normal version, meanwhile, appears to help protect neurons from damage involving amyloid, a protein that can accumulate abnormally in the brains of people with Alzheimer's.

"These peptides are emerging as key regulators of aging biology," Cohen said. "They connect mitochondrial function to diseases like Alzheimer's and heart disease and now, potentially, to nutrition."

A Hidden Mechanism for Protecting the Heart

The scientists also identified a potentially important connection between humanin and an enzyme called Nox2, which helps generate reactive oxygen species.

Although these molecules have useful roles in normal cell signaling and immune defense, excessive production can contribute to oxidative stress and damage blood vessels and other tissues.

The researchers observed that people with higher humanin levels tended to have lower Nox2 activity. This relationship raises the possibility that humanin helps limit damaging oxidative processes, potentially offering an additional layer of cardiovascular protection.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that the Mediterranean diet could support heart health in two complementary ways. The diet may help reduce oxidative stress directly while also supporting the production of mitochondrial microproteins that influence pathways involved in cellular damage.

However, the observed associations do not establish that the diet directly increases these proteins or that the proteins themselves prevent cardiovascular disease.

"This could represent a new cardioprotective mechanism of the Mediterranean diet," Vicinanza said.

Bringing the Mediterranean Diet to a Global Audience

Vicinanza's interest in the Mediterranean diet extends beyond investigating its effects inside the body. He has also worked to promote this traditional eating pattern internationally as a way to support human health, cultural heritage, and environmental sustainability.

As part of those efforts, he collaborated with the Municipality of Pollica in Italy, which is recognized as a UNESCO Mediterranean Diet emblematic community.

That collaboration helped support the establishment of the International Day of the Mediterranean Diet through the United Nations.

Observed every year on November 16, the international event is intended to draw attention to the Mediterranean diet's health benefits as well as its cultural traditions and environmental significance.

For Vicinanza, the new findings reinforce the relationship between traditional food practices and modern discoveries about how the body functions.

"We're connecting centuries-old dietary traditions with cutting-edge molecular biology," Vicinanza said. "It supports the idea that healthy eating patterns with little to no ultra-processed foods reflect how humans have eaten over long periods and may create conditions to which mitochondria -- ancient cellular organelles -- are likely adapted."

Could Tiny Proteins Help Unlock Healthier Aging?

Although the findings are promising, the researchers emphasize that the study was relatively small and observational. That means it identified relationships between dietary habits and biological measurements but could not determine whether eating a Mediterranean diet directly caused the differences in microprotein levels.

Other factors, including participants' overall health and lifestyle, could also influence the results.

Nevertheless, the discovery opens an intriguing possibility for the emerging field of precision nutrition, which seeks to develop dietary recommendations based on an individual's biological characteristics and needs.

If future research confirms that dietary changes can reliably influence humanin, SHMOOSE, and related microproteins, these molecules could potentially become useful tools for evaluating nutritional interventions and developing more personalized strategies for healthy aging.

The next step is to determine whether adopting a Mediterranean-style diet actually increases these proteins and whether those changes lead to measurable improvements in cardiovascular health, brain function, or disease risk.

"Our goal is to move from observing associations to understanding causality," Vicinanza said. "If we can harness these pathways, we may be able to design nutritional strategies that promote healthy aging at the molecular level."

The work was funded by the USC Daryl and Irwin Simon Nutrition for Alzheimer's Disease Prevention Research Fund (to Vicinanza), the Hanson-Thorell Family Research Award (to Vicinanza), National Institutes of Health grant P30AG094848 (to Cohen) and PRIN 2022 grant 000031_23_PP_PIGNATELLI_PRIN_2022-B53D23021240006 (to Pignatelli).

#5755. MazeBolt launches native RADAR deployment for Akamai DDoS protection customers

Distributed denial-of-service testing company MazeBolt Technologies Ltd. today launched a native deployment of its RADAR validation platform for customers of Akamai Technologies Inc.

Enterprises using Akamai’s DDoS protection can have continuous testing running within hours without taking services offline. The release targets the configuration gaps that open up as a company adds services, application programming interfaces and regions behind its DDoS protection.

Akamai setups are rarely tested independently against each of those changes, according to MazeBolt, and a gap can stay hidden until an attack reaches a login page or a payment flow. Founder and Chief Executive Matthew Andriani said testing “even a few times a year cannot keep pace” now that artificial intelligence projects keep adding new services and APIs.

Akamai’s own State of the Internet report, published in March, found that Layer 7 DDoS attacks rose 104% over two years, and the company blamed part of that growth on attack tools that use AI to make web applications and APIs easier to hit.

RADAR fires simulated attacks at Akamai-protected services from inside the customer’s own environment. The attack library covers known vectors as well as the AI-orchestrated and AI-generated attacks MazeBolt added with its VectorAI module in June. When RADAR first tests a production environment, about 37% of attack vectors get past the protection already in place, based on MazeBolt’s data from initial deployments.

Each run ends in a report with remediation guidance written for the specific protection vendor, and RADAR repeats the test once a fix is in place. “Deployed protection is not proven protection,” said Eyal Rahimi, vice president of engineering at MazeBolt. Customers also need to be able to prove which gaps they have closed, Rahimi said.

Most financial institutions test far less often. In a MazeBolt survey of 300 of their security leaders last year, 86% said they test their DDoS defenses once a year or less. Akamai reported in May that the median duration of Layers 3 and 4 DDoS attacks on the sector has risen 738% since 2024.

John Grady, chief analyst at Omdia, said misconfigurations and out-of-date rules remain the source of many security incidents. “DDoS is no different,” Grady said. “It is a critical area where security teams must ensure protection is current, because successful attacks impact availability and directly affect the bottom line.”

Native Layer 7 support for Akamai environments is available today to all RADAR customers. Cloudflare Inc., F5 Inc. and Radware Ltd. are among the other mitigation vendors whose products RADAR already tests across scrubbing centers, on-premises equipment and cloud services.

#5754. Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans

Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Another open enrollment period is set to begin on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, and the team at Oscar Health is focusing on the unique ways it can innovate in the turbulent market.

Oscar is growing the number of counties in its geographic footprint by 24% in 2027, offering plans across 713 counties in 21 states. It is also investing in new specialized plans, such as its RetireEase offering, and in expanding coverage options designed for individuals with certain conditions.

Janet Liang, president of Oscar Insurance, told Fierce Healthcare that it's critical for plans to learn as much as they can about the individual consumer, so that they can shape benefits that effectively meet the needs of the people who are coming to the marketplaces for coverage.

"We are completely dialed in to the individual consumer," she said. "We know the people who are in the ACA, and it's a broad, broad range of people. It's not one size fits all, and what we do is we spend the time to understand who comes into the ACA and what are the services and needs that individuals have."

That includes putting a focus on collecting plenty of feedback from existing members, and what they're searching for as existing enrollees, as well as collecting data on broader consumer behaviors on the exchanges.

The RetireEase plan, for example, was born from this thinking, Liang said. The offering, which is launching in five states next year, aims to support members in the transition to Medicare coverage, targeted to people aged 55 to 64.

Benefits include set prices for key services in this age range, from preventive care to physical therapy to cardiology. Members that enroll in RetireEase can also access specific supports designed for the handoff to Medicare, for caregivers and transportation if needed.

Liang said this population tends to have unique concerns about affordability as employers shift their approaches in a way that is leading more people to retire early, leaving them on a fixed income. It's also an age range where people begin to develop challenging chronic conditions that will need to be managed in the future.

The team took that feedback and those particular needs it heart when building out RetireEase, Liang said.

Oscar's suite of specialized offerings includes some of its most popular plans, she said. In addition to the new launch, Oscar is expanding the reach of its existing specialized plans. HelloMeno, its plan designed for women navigating menopause, will grow to 15 states by 2027, for example.

Liang said that these plans have higher Net Promoter Scores than its traditional plans, and they also tend to have higher retention rates than the broader offerings.

"Based on the retention rate and the high NPS scores, we know that we're meeting an unmet need," she said.

And the Oscar team is already planning for the future around these specialized plans, and has determined where to go next for 2028. Expanding this slate is a central part of Oscar's broader strategy around the ACA, which also includes enhancements to bronze, silver and gold plans as well as a focus on individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRA.

ICHRA plans have rebranded as Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense, or CHOICE. But in these models, an employer offers workers a stipend to purchase an exchange plan, rather than offering coverage directly.

Liang said Oscar believes this is an area that will continue to grow. She said that they're seeing higher numbers of employers requesting quotes for potential CHOICE arrangements, and Oscar has doubled its membership between 2025 and 2026.

She added that Oscar expects to triple its CHOICE market share by 2029.

"So there's an obvious interest by employers to reduce their costs," Liang said. "And we also look at markets where there's just a lot of interest by both small employers, regional employers, to just start off. What you see is new employers and new companies that are forming will go straight to CHOICE instead of starting on the traditional insurance path."

Stay up to date on the latest across Washington, D.C. with this weekly brief. Read below for news from Oct. 26 to Oct. 30.

HHS’ Office on Women’s Health (OWH) announced Tuesday a coordinated initiative with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and DenseBreast-info.org (DBI) to improve breast cancer screening and early detection efforts nationwide.

The OWH–AHRQ Breast Cancer Screening and Diagnostic Follow-up Initiative will analyze national screening and follow-up patterns, with more than 40 health systems poised to expand evidence-based practices and address delays in care.

“Women deserve clear information about breast cancer screening options beyond mammography, particularly if they have dense breasts or other risk factors,” said Tammy Huizenga, AHRQ senior advisor for nutrition and women’s health, in a statement. “Understanding their individual risk and available options helps women and their healthcare providers make informed decisions that support earlier detection.”

OWH and DBI will also collaborate through a memorandum of understanding to expand access to evidence-based educational resources aimed at supporting informed discussions between women and providers, promote understanding of screenings and diagnostic follow-up options, and improve breast density awareness.

HHS' health information technology arm finalized a rule that streamlines the health IT certification program, projecting to save billions in compliance costs.

The rule, called Health Data, Technology and Interoperability: ONC Deregulatory Actions to Unleash Prosperity (HTI-5), is projected to save more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs, according to the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC). Full story.

The Trump administration awarded $233 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across California. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through regional care networks, telehealth, workforce development and upgraded healthcare technology. California has committed its full fiscal year 2026 funding to improve healthcare in rural communities across the state.

The state plans to use the investment to expand rural primary, maternal, specialty and behavioral healthcare; grow the healthcare workforce; expand telehealth and regional care networks; modernize technology and infrastructure; and support new care delivery and payment models, according to a CMS announcement. Regional care networks and telehealth will connect patients with providers and help coordinate care, while partnerships with midwives, doulas and community health workers will support maternal and primary care. Investments will also support education and training pathways to grow the rural healthcare workforce, improve technology and modernize infrastructure.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

CMS doled out $193.7M in RHTP funding to 45 organizations across Florida to expand healthcare access in rural communities, with a particular focus on bringing care closer to patients.

Florida will use the substantial investment to build out telehealth, remote monitoring, mobile and community-based services; increase access to preventive and specialty care; strengthen rural providers and the healthcare workforce; and support new care delivery and payment models.

The state's approach uses telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based services, diagnostic kiosks and community paramedicine to give patients more ways to access needed care. Partnerships are a defining feature of Florida’s approach, with more than 500 partnerships across the 45 awardees bringing hospitals, clinics, local governments and community organizations together to support statewide rural healthcare transformation, according to CMS in an Oct. 23 announcement.

Florida will receive $209,938,195 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

CMS awarded $186 million in funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through modern technology, new care models, an expanded healthcare workforce and improvements to healthcare facilities, the agency announced.

The investment supports five initiatives designed to strengthen healthcare delivery and modernize rural Idaho’s healthcare system. Funding for telehealth, cybersecurity and electronic health record modernization will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care better locally. Investments in community health workers and emergency medical services professionals will help bring services into homes and communities, while training, recruitment and retention efforts will grow Idaho’s rural healthcare workforce. The funding will also support programs addressing chronic disease, behavioral health, maternal and child health as well as improvements to rural healthcare facilities and equipment.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents. Full story

CMS awarded $87 million in RHTP funding to 129 rural healthcare providers through Rural Texas Strong to strengthen healthcare across rural communities. The investment will help improve health outcomes for rural Texans, build a strong healthcare workforce and modernize facilities and equipment across rural Texas, according to an agency announcement.

The funding will help rural providers prevent and manage chronic conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic respiratory disease; recruit and retain physicians, emergency medical personnel and other healthcare professionals; replace aging medical equipment; and improve existing facilities. A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said. Full story

The investment will support 26 rural healthcare providers as they renovate, reconfigure, equip or repurpose existing facilities and expand maternal health, behavioral health, diagnostic, outpatient and chronic disease management services across Missouri, according to an announcement.

The funding will support new labor, delivery and private triage rooms; expanded behavioral health services for older adults and people with substance use disorders; and upgraded diagnostic equipment, including MRI, mammography and ultrasound services. The funding will also expand primary care and increase the capacity of rural health clinics, helping rural providers update existing facilities and capabilities to better match the healthcare needs of the communities they serve, CMS said.

In total, Mississippi will receive $216,276,818 during fiscal year 2026.

The state plans to invest in virtual and specialty care, mobile health services and chronic disease management, growing the rural healthcare workforce and modernizing technology and health data systems.

The investment will support new tools and services across the state, including mobile health units and drone delivery for time-critical medical supplies; remote eye care and patient monitoring technology; nursing education and apprenticeship programs; and secure systems that allow healthcare providers to better share information. Investments will also support mental health and substance use disorder recovery services and tools that reduce administrative burden for healthcare professionals, CMS announced.

West Virginia will receive a total of $199,476,099 in RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.
